case_title: Dharamdas Nandlal Mehta & Anr. vs Meridian Construction Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dharamdas Nandlal Mehta & Anr. are the Appellants/Petitioners, and Meridian Construction Pvt. Ltd. and Harresh N. Mehta are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying dispute concerning the alteration, renovation, and development of an immovable property known as 'Hendre House, Girgaon', Mumbai. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; matter pertains to oppression, mismanagement, and unauthorized alteration of immovable corporate property. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Mumbai passed interim orders on 13 January 2017 (IA No. 03/2016 in TCP No. 31/(MAH)/2015) and an injunction order on 8 February 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLAT had issued an interim restraint on 23 February 2017 prohibiting construction/alteration; Respondent No. 2 filed an affidavit on 20 March 2017 justifying actions, which was rejected. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Dissatisfied with NCLT's interim orders, Appellants moved NCLAT; during appeal, repeated adjournments were sought for settlement, which failed to culminate in final terms.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal should keep interlocutory appeals pending indefinitely for settlement discussions, or remit the matter to the lower tribunal with directions to maintain status quo and decide the main company petition on merits.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Prolonged interim proceedings should not delay the final adjudication of a company petition; where interim protections adequately balance party interests, the appellate court should remand the matter for expeditious final determination. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The tribunal must balance equity by safeguarding the subject property while ensuring the primary company petition and pending contempt proceedings are adjudicated without undue delay. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where parties repeatedly seek extensions without finalizing settlement terms, further adjournments must be refused to avoid procedural abuse. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that its interim protective order should remain operative until the NCLT finally disposes of the company petition, remitting the matter accordingly.
operative_order: Both appeals stand disposed of; interim order of 23 February 2017 to continue until the NCLT finally decides the company petition; NCLT directed to adjudicate the petition on merits or record settlement if filed, and dispose of contempt proceedings if an unconditional apology is tendered.
summary: Appellants Dharamdas Nandlal Mehta and another appealed against interim orders of NCLT Mumbai concerning alterations to 'Hendre House, Girgaon' in an oppression and mismanagement petition. While the NCLAT had earlier restrained construction, the parties repeatedly sought adjournments to negotiate a settlement. Refusing further delay, the NCLAT ruled that protracted settlement talks should not stall justice. It ordered its interim restraint to remain in effect until NCLT Mumbai finally disposes of the company petition on merits, and remitted the matter while granting liberty to file settlement terms if finalized.

case_title: M/s Goldstar Enclave Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs Devinder Singh Shant & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Goldstar Enclave Pvt. Ltd. and its co-promoters are Appellants, and Devinder Singh Shant & Ors. are Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial real estate operations regarding the sale and leasing of shops, cinema hall, multiplexes, and restaurants in 'Globe Shopping Centertainment'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; dispute concerns management, property disposition, and signing authorities of company bank accounts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The appeal arose from an NCLT order passed in January 2017 in Company Petition No. 49 of 2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The parties executed and submitted agreed terms for property monetization, joint bank account operations, advertisement in three newspapers, and revenue-sharing mechanisms. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT passed an order in CP No. 49 of 2016, which was appealed in Company Appeal (AT) No. 32 of 2017; the parties formulated a mutual interim working arrangement before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal can formalize a consent arrangement governing company asset management and bank account operations to maintain corporate functioning pending the final adjudication of an oppression petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To prevent the stalling of commercial enterprises during shareholder litigation, the tribunal may adopt consensual operational frameworks that balance control, preserve assets, and protect business continuity. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Section 422 of the Companies Act 2013, company petitions must be prosecuted and determined expeditiously, and interim asset management mechanisms should facilitate, rather than obstruct, the main trial. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on mutual consent of all contesting factions to establish transparency through joint bank operations and public advertisements. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the appeal should be disposed of by substituting the impugned order with the agreed interim arrangement, directing expeditious trial of the company petition.
operative_order: Order of January 2017 modified in terms of the agreed 11-point interim framework; parties directed to cooperate with the NCLT for early disposal under Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013; appeal stands disposed of with no costs.
summary: In a shareholder dispute regarding M/s Goldstar Enclave Pvt. Ltd. and its commercial complex 'Globe Shopping Centertainment', the parties appealed an NCLT interim order in CP No. 49 of 2016. Before the NCLAT, the parties reached an agreed interim framework governing the leasing/sale of units, public advertisements, escrow arrangements, and joint operation of bank accounts. The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by substituting the impugned order with these agreed terms and directing the NCLT to expedite the final hearing of the petition in accordance with Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013.

case_title: Siddharth Nahata vs Billets Elektro Werke Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Siddharth Nahata, Director of Tryst Industries Pvt. Ltd., is the Appellant/Corporate Debtor; Billets Elektro Werke Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent/Operational Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A principal-dealer arrangement where the Appellant was to sell articles received from the Respondent and make payments upon execution of purchase orders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor claimed an outstanding debt of Rs. 33.78 lakhs, inclusive of overdue interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A Section 8 demand notice was sent on 22 May 2017, to which the Appellant replied on 7 June 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant produced prior correspondence from 20 July 2016 and 3 August 2016, alongside a criminal complaint, demonstrating a pre-existing dispute regarding the Respondent violating dealership terms by selling directly in the Appellant's territory. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 9 application on 8 September 2017. The Appellant challenged this, arguing that a valid dispute existed prior to the demand notice.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 insolvency application can be admitted when correspondence and admissions establish a genuine, pre-existing dispute over business conduct prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority must reject an insolvency application under Section 9 if there is substantive evidence of a real, pre-existing dispute between the parties before the issuance of the demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and 9 of the IBC mandate that operational creditors cannot initiate CIRP if the corporate debtor raises a plausible dispute supported by historical correspondence. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on pre-notice letters from July and August 2016 and the Respondent's own admission in their counter-affidavit confirming the principal-dealer relationship to validate the dispute's existence. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that a valid prior dispute existed, meaning the Section 9 application should not have been admitted.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The impugned order admitting the Insolvency Resolution Process is quashed and set aside. Further proceedings are stopped. No orders as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT's admission of a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by Billets Elektro Werke Pvt. Ltd.. Although the parties reached a compromise during the appeal, the NCLAT evaluated the case on merits. Finding clear evidence of a pre-existing dispute regarding their dealership agreement prior to the Section 8 notice, the NCLAT allowed the appeal and quashed the insolvency proceedings.

case_title: Design Worx Infrastructure India Pvt. Ltd. vs Premier Restaurants Private Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Design Worx Infrastructure India Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant/Operational Creditor, and Premier Restaurants Private Ltd. is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Operational Creditor was assigned a job work contract initially valued at Rs. 95 lakhs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid amounts with the Corporate Debtor alleging unilateral escalations without approval and claiming liquidated damages for delays capped at 10% of the contract. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Execution was originally slated for 31 July 2015, extended to January 2016, and eventually handed over in March 2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor produced emails dated 4 May 2016 and 17 May 2017 showing dissatisfaction with the work (unresolved snags), proof of engaging a third party to finish the job, and rent liabilities of Rs. 11 lakhs incurred due to the handover delay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench rejected the Section 9 application on 8 May 2017 in C.P. No. (IB)-76 (ND)/2017, determining that a dispute existed between the parties.
legal_issues: Whether documented dissatisfaction regarding job execution, unresolved snags, and financial losses due to project delays constitute a valid 'existence of dispute' barring a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor's insolvency petition is not maintainable if the corporate debtor establishes a pre-existing dispute regarding service quality or execution delays. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(6) defining 'dispute' includes contestations over the quality of goods or services, making claims of unresolved snags and resultant damages sufficient to reject a Section 9 petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found that pre-notice emails demanding snag rectification, engagement of third-party contractors, and documented rent liabilities adequately proved the existence of a dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed the Adjudicating Authority's specific finding that a dispute existed prior to the demand notice, rendering the appeal meritless.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit.
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed the NCLT's rejection of its Section 9 insolvency application against Premier Restaurants Pvt. Ltd.. The Corporate Debtor provided emails demonstrating dissatisfaction with the job work, project delays causing rent liabilities, and the necessity of hiring third parties to rectify unremoved snags. The NCLAT upheld the rejection, confirming that these elements clearly established a pre-existing dispute under the IBC.

case_title: Mitcon Consultancy & Engineering Services Ltd. vs Al-Ameen Green Energy Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mitcon Consultancy & Engineering Services Ltd. is the Appellant; Al-Ameen Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debt arising from a work order issued by the Respondent. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed outstanding dues that were liable to be paid prior to filing the Section 9 application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The underlying work order was dated 18 May 2015. The NCLT rejected the Section 9 application on 23 October 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Paragraph 7 of the work order dated 18 May 2015 clearly outlined the payment terms demonstrating maturity. Furthermore, no dispute existed prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai rejected the Section 9 application, classifying the claim as premature. The Operational Creditor appealed, and the Respondent failed to appear.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can dismiss a Section 9 application as premature when documentary evidence confirms the debt payment had matured, and whether a dispute raised for the first time in reply to a Section 8 notice prevents CIRP initiation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency application cannot be dismissed as premature if the underlying contract or work order explicitly establishes that the payment date had passed before the application's filing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A valid 'dispute' under the IBC must exist prior to the receipt of the Section 8 demand notice; raising a dispute merely in response to the notice is insufficient. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied heavily on the written 'Terms of payment' in the work order, determining that the NCLT had ignored plain documentary evidence in favor of baseless statements by the corporate debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the debt had matured and the Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate the factual record, necessitating reversal.
operative_order: The NCLT order dated 23 October 2017 is set aside. The case is remitted to NCLT Chennai to admit the application if complete after notice, or to grant the Appellant time to cure defects. No costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT Chennai order that rejected its Section 9 IBC application as premature. The NCLAT found that the Adjudicating Authority failed to examine the payment terms in the May 2015 work order, which clearly proved the debt had matured. Furthermore, the Corporate Debtor raised a dispute only after receiving the Section 8 notice. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and remitted the matter for admission.

case_title: Brahmani Infratech Pvt Ltd & Ors vs Malaxmi Infra Ventures (India) Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Brahmani Infratech Pvt Ltd & Ors are the Appellants. Malaxmi Infra Ventures (India) Ltd is the 1st Respondent, and Mr. Y. Harish Chandra Prasad is the 2nd Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Disputes involving corporate directorship and allegations of oppression and mismanagement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; pertains to maintainability of an oppression and mismanagement petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT passed the impugned order in CP No. 42/2011 on 31 January 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLAT had already affirmed in a prior order (dated 23 March 2017 in AT No. 78 of 2017) that the company petition was unmaintainable with respect to the 2nd Respondent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad ruled the company petition was only maintainable for the 1st Respondent and that the 2nd Respondent lacked locus standi. Incongruously, the NCLT ordered the Appellant company to appoint the 2nd Respondent as a Director. The Appellants appealed this specific direction.
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal can validly grant substantive affirmative relief (such as directing appointment as a Director) to a petitioner whom it concurrently found lacked locus standi to maintain the petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicating authority cannot grant substantive relief to a party within a proceeding if it has explicitly determined that the party lacks the locus standi to maintain the petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relief under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act is strictly contingent upon the maintainability of the petition; non-maintainability strips the tribunal of jurisdiction to issue directions favoring the unqualified party. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the logical contradiction in the NCLT's own order and its prior appellate validation of the non-maintainability finding to strike down the relief. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that directing the company to appoint a party found to lack standing was legally unjustified.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. Clause (iv) of the impugned judgment directing the appointment of the second petitioner as a Director is set aside. Interim orders vacated. No order as to costs.
summary: Brahmani Infratech Pvt Ltd appealed a contradictory NCLT Hyderabad order regarding an oppression and mismanagement petition. The NCLT had ruled the petition was only maintainable for the 1st Respondent and that the 2nd Respondent lacked locus standi, yet it inexplicably ordered the company to appoint the 2nd Respondent as a Director. The NCLAT set aside this specific direction, reasoning that substantive relief cannot be granted to a party whose petition was held unmaintainable.

case_title: Bhikhunhai J. Patel & Anr vs Hetshri Dairy Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bhikhunhai J. Patel and another are the Appellants/Petitioners, and Hetshri Dairy Pvt. Ltd. and others are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter pertains to a dispute over shareholding and membership within the Respondent company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is an oppression and mismanagement case. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Specific timeline dates of earlier notices are not detailed in the text. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT evaluated the Annual Return and Form No. 2, which demonstrated the Appellants did not possess the requisite 1/10th shares or 1/10th membership. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed the original petition (TP No. 74/397-398/NCLT/AHM/2016) on 5th April 2017 on the ground that the Appellants lacked the eligibility criteria to file under Sections 397 and 398.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellants held the requisite 1/10th shareholding to maintain a petition for oppression and mismanagement under the Companies Act, 1956.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petition for oppression and mismanagement is not maintainable if the petitioners fail to establish the threshold requirement of holding one-tenth of the issued share capital or representing one-tenth of the total members. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act require strict compliance with the numerical threshold for eligibility. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bald allegations of fabricated annual returns cannot be accepted without a substantive documentary record proving the requisite shareholding on the date of filing. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal held that the Appellants lacked the statutory minimum 1/10th shares to sustain the petition, warranting dismissal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and there shall be no order as to cost.
summary: In this company appeal, the Appellants challenged an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing their petition for oppression and mismanagement. The core issue was whether the Appellants held the mandatory 1/10th shareholding required under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956. The NCLAT upheld the lower tribunal's finding, noting that the company's Annual Return and Form No. 2 indicated the Appellants did not meet the required membership threshold. Rejecting the Appellants' unsupported claims that the returns were fabricated, the NCLAT concluded that disputed questions of fact regarding eligibility without corroborating records could not yield relief, ultimately dismissing the appeal for lack of merit.

case_title: Sudha Commercial Company Ltd vs Milkfood Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sudha Commercial Company Ltd is the Appellant/Petitioner, and Milkfood Ltd. & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute involves internal corporate amendments concerning shareholding changes and a specific land transaction. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No financial debt default metric is applicable in this limitation dispute. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The contested land transaction occurred in the year 2007, making it a subject of limitation scrutiny during the 2016-2017 proceedings. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal reviewed the amendment applications (Nos. 21 and 9 of 2016) against the historical timeline of the 2007 land transaction. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh partly allowed an amendment petition (Company Petition No. 28/Chd/PB./2016) on 27th June 2017, but rejected the portion concerning the 2007 land transaction.
legal_issues: Whether the amendment prayer regarding a land transaction from 2007 is barred by the laws of limitation under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Claims relating to transactions that fall outside the statutory limitation period cannot be introduced via an amendment to a company petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 governs limitation periods for proceedings before the Tribunal, thereby barring stale claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal calculated the time elapsed since the 2007 transaction to determine if the claim survived the limitation period. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the part of the amendment seeking relief for a 2007 land transaction was rightly rejected as time-barred, affirming the lower tribunal's selective allowance of the amendment.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, with liberty open to the appellant to raise validly pleaded issues regarding shareholding changes during the final hearing. There shall be no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT Chandigarh order that partially allowed their amendment petition against Milkfood Ltd. The core issue focused on the NCLT's refusal to permit amendments concerning a land transaction from 2007. The NCLAT evaluated this under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013, which governs limitation. It determined that introducing a decade-old transaction was fundamentally barred by limitation. Consequently, the NCLAT affirmed the lower tribunal's decision to reject that specific part of the amendment, dismissing the appeal while clarifying that validly pleaded shareholding issues could still be pursued during the final hearing.

case_title: Yogendra Yasupal vs M/S. Jigsaw Solutions & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Jigsaw Solutions is the Operational Creditor, the 2nd Respondent is the Corporate Debtor, and Yogendra Yasupal is the Appellant/Director. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of services by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default triggered a Section 9 application; exact financial metrics are not detailed in the text. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor failed to raise a dispute regarding service quality upon receiving the Section 8 demand notice. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant relied on an anticipatory bail order from the Madras High Court to allege a pre-existing dispute, while the Operational Creditor's application was deemed complete. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai admitted the Section 9 application (Company Petition No. 559/(IB)/CB/2017) and declared a moratorium on 15th September 2017, which the Appellant challenged.
legal_issues: Whether observations against individual officers in a court order or internal communications constitute an 'existence of dispute' to bar the admission of a Section 9 petition under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: General observations against individual officers in unrelated court orders do not constitute a pre-existing dispute regarding a corporate debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2) of the IBC mandates that a dispute must be explicitly raised regarding the quality of goods or services prior to the demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal evaluates whether a specific, written objection about service quality was raised directly by the Corporate Debtor in response to the Section 8 notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since no written objection regarding service quality was made at the Section 8(2) stage, the anticipatory bail order did not demonstrate a valid statutory dispute, justifying admission of the petition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost.
summary: This insolvency appeal involves a Corporate Debtor's director challenging the admission of a Section 9 IBC petition filed by Operational Creditor M/s. Jigsaw Solutions. NCLT Chennai had previously admitted the petition and initiated a moratorium. The Appellant argued that a pre-existing dispute existed, citing an anticipatory bail order from the Madras High Court. The NCLAT rejected this argument, ruling that isolated court observations against individuals do not amount to a valid dispute under the Code. Relying on the Supreme Court's Mobilox Innovations ruling, the NCLAT noted the Corporate Debtor failed to raise specific written objections regarding service quality during the Section 8 notice stage, thereby dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Sak Industries Pvt Ltd vs Fenance Auto Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: SAK Industries Pvt Ltd is the Appellant/Operational Creditor, and Fenance Auto Ltd is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational debt underlying a Section 9 insolvency application. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount and date are not detailed. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The core timeline issue was the statutory 7-day period mandated to remove defects in an IBC application. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The primary evidentiary document relied upon was the Supreme Court judgment in M/s Surendra Trading Company, which interpreted the defect-removal timeline. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi rejected the Section 9 application on 19th July 2017 specifically because the Appellant failed to remove application defects within the mandated 7-day window.
legal_issues: Whether the 7-day timeline prescribed under the IBC for removing defects in an insolvency application is mandatory or directory.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory time limit of seven days granted to an applicant to rectify defects in an insolvency petition is directory, not mandatory. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Provisos to Sections 7(5), 9(5), and 10(4) of the IBC regarding the 7-day period for curing defects do not act as strict bars that automatically invalidate a petition if breached. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied entirely on the binding precedent established by the Supreme Court in 'M/s Surendra Trading Company', overturning earlier rigid interpretations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench ruled that the lower tribunal erred in rejecting the petition solely for missing the 7-day defect removal window, and that the applicant must be granted an opportunity to cure defects.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 19th July 2017 is set aside, and the case is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority to allow the appellant time to remove defects. There shall be no order as to cost.
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed the rejection of its Section 9 insolvency petition by NCLT New Delhi. The lower tribunal had dismissed the petition because the Creditor failed to cure application defects within the 7-day statutory period, treating the deadline as mandatory. The NCLAT examined the appeal in light of a recent Supreme Court judgment in M/s Surendra Trading Company, which clarified that the 7-day timeline under IBC Sections 7, 9, and 10 is directory, not mandatory. Applying this binding ruling, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's dismissal, allowed the appeal, and remanded the matter, directing the Adjudicating Authority to grant the Appellant time to rectify the defects.

case_title: Anand Kumar & Ors vs Usha Kumar & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anand Kumar and others are the Appellants, and Usha Kumar and others are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An internal corporate dispute concerning a poorly functioning company leading to an interim NCLT order. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No financial default metrics apply to this procedural dispute. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original interim order was passed on 6th March 2017; the amendment application was filed more than 90 days later, exceeding the 30-day limit. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal evaluated the chronology of the filings and determined there was no substantive error in the original March 6 order warranting correction. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed Interlocutory Application No. 236 of 2017, refusing to amend the interim order originally passed in IA No. 72 of 2015.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT possesses the jurisdiction to review or recall its interim orders beyond the 30-day statutory limit in the absence of a patent error.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The National Company Law Tribunal lacks the inherent jurisdiction to review or recall its own orders, except to correct apparent errors within a strict 30-day window. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 155 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 strictly confines the power to rectify errors to a 30-day limitation period from the date of the original order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The bench assessed the timing of the application (filed after 90 days) and the absence of any visible illegality or perversity in the original interim order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that since the application was filed well beyond the 30-day limit and there was no factual error in the original order, no interference was justified.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. Parties are directed to co-operate with the Tribunal for the expeditious disposal of the Company Petition, preferably within three months. No order as to cost.
summary: The Appellants challenged an NCLT Kolkata order that refused to amend an interim order passed three months prior. The dispute centered on whether the tribunal could review its earlier decision based on an alleged error. The NCLAT noted that the NCLT lacks general powers to review or recall its orders, except via inherent powers under Rule 11 or 155 of the NCLT Rules to correct errors within 30 days. Because the Appellants filed their interlocutory application after 90 days, and the NCLAT found no actual error or perversity in the original interim order, the appeal was dismissed. The NCLAT directed expedited disposal of the main pending petition.

case_title: Pallavi Gems Pvt Ltd & Anr vs M/S Haresh N Mataliya & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pallavi Gems Pvt Ltd & Anr are the Appellants, and M/S Haresh N Mataliya & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute regarding a company petition initially filed before the erstwhile Company Law Board. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 came into force on June 1, 2016, after the original petition was filed. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The maintainability of the Company Petition was challenged on the grounds of limitation under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT rejected the interlocutory application challenging the petition's maintainability on limitation grounds, which prompted this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the period of limitation prescribed under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 is applicable retroactively to a company petition filed before the erstwhile Company Law Board before the section came into force.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory provisions regarding limitation do not apply retroactively to petitions already pending before the implementation of those provisions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013, establishing limitation periods, was not applicable to petitions filed before the Company Law Board prior to June 1, 2016. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified the date of filing against the effective date of the statute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellate Tribunal held that the petition was maintainable and could not be dismissed on limitation grounds, thereby upholding the NCLT's order.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal declined to interfere with the impugned order, effectively dismissing the appeal.
summary: The Appellants challenged an NCLT order that rejected their application to dismiss a pending company petition on the grounds of limitation. The NCLAT observed that the original petition was filed before the erstwhile Company Law Board prior to Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 coming into force on June 1, 2016. Consequently, the limitation rules of Section 433 did not apply retroactively to the case. Finding no error in the lower tribunal's decision that the petition was maintainable, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: K Ishwara Bhatt vs M/S Sun Pharmaceutical Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: K. Ishwara Bhatt is the Appellant, and M/s Sun Pharmaceutical Ltd. & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed; dispute pertains to territorial jurisdiction for a company petition. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The registered office of the respondent company is located in the State of Gujarat (Ahmedabad). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, passed an order on January 25, 2017, transferring C.P.No. 61/59/2015 to the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench for lack of territorial jurisdiction in Delhi.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT Principal Bench has territorial jurisdiction to hear a company petition when the respondent company's registered office is located in the State of Gujarat.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Territorial jurisdiction over a company rests exclusively with the NCLT Bench that governs the state where the company's registered office is located. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 434(1)(a) read with Section 419(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, and Rule 64 of the NCLT Rules establish that jurisdiction is determined solely by the location of the registered office. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the undisputed fact that the registered office of the respondent is in Ahmedabad. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the company is registered in Gujarat, the NCLAT affirmed that only the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench possesses territorial jurisdiction over the matter.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to cost, and the parties are directed to cooperate with NCLT Ahmedabad for the early disposal of the Company Petition.
summary: The Appellant challenged an order by the NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, which transferred their company petition to the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench. The core issue was territorial jurisdiction, as the respondent company's registered office is in Gujarat. Relying on statutory provisions and the precedent set in '63 Moons Technology Limited', the NCLAT held that Benches, including the Principal Bench, have territorial jurisdiction exclusively based on the location of a company's registered office. Finding no ground to interfere with the transfer, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal and directed cooperation for early disposal.

case_title: Prabir Mukherjee vs M/s. Jatia Cotton Mills Limited & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prabir Mukherjee is the Appellant (a respondent in the original CP), and M/s. Jatia Cotton Mills Limited & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not applicable; dispute centers on procedural clubbing of multiple company petitions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant requested three company petitions be heard together because the parties were common, but the reliefs sought in the petitions were not identical. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected C.A. No. 87 of 2017 on July 11, 2017, refusing to tie the cases together due to non-identical reliefs.
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal is obligated to club and hear multiple company petitions together solely because the parties are common, despite differing reliefs.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The decision to consolidate and hear multiple petitions together is a discretionary power of the Tribunal, dependent on the nature of the cases and identicality of reliefs. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 does not mandate appellate interference in a Tribunal's procedural discretion regarding case management unless there is an apparent illegality. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined whether the reliefs sought across the three petitions were identical to warrant a joint hearing. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since deciding whether to hear petitions together or separately falls within the Tribunal's discretion and there was no illegality, interference was unwarranted.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged a procedural order by the NCLT Kolkata Bench that refused to club three company petitions together for a joint hearing. Although the parties in the petitions were common, the NCLT noted that the reliefs sought were not identical. The NCLAT upheld this decision, stating that the choice to hear cases together or separately is inherently up to the Tribunal's discretion, based on the nature of the case and the specific reliefs. Finding no illegality in the lower tribunal's exercise of its discretion, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Abro Technologies (P) Ltd vs Delhi Warehousing Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Abro Technologies (P) Ltd. is the Appellant, and M/s. Delhi Warehousing Pvt. Ltd. & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate dispute regarding the reduction of the Appellant's shareholding. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant's shareholding was reduced below 10% in the year 2008, yet the petition was filed approximately eight years later. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal observed that there was an unexplained delay of eight years before the Appellant approached the judicial authority. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, dismissed the Company Petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 on December 22, 2016, citing delay and laches.
legal_issues: Whether a petition for oppression and mismanagement is maintainable when filed after an unexplained delay of eight years from the cause of action.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petition alleging oppression and mismanagement must be filed within a reasonable period; significant, unexplained delays will result in dismissal due to laches. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Equitable remedies under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 are barred if the petitioner sleeps on their rights for an unreasonable timeframe. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal assessed the timeline from the 2008 share reduction to the filing date, noting the complete lack of explanation for the eight-year gap. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Appellant's failure to move the erstwhile Company Law Board within a reasonable time constituted laches, thereby justifying the petition's rejection.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit.
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT Principal Bench's dismissal of their company petition filed under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956. The dispute arose from the Appellant's shareholding being reduced below 10% in 2008. However, the Appellant waited approximately eight years before initiating legal action, without providing any grounds to explain this significant delay. The NCLAT affirmed the lower tribunal's decision, ruling that the equitable relief sought was barred by severe delay and laches. Consequently, finding no merit in the case, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Sri Haridas Pottath vs Peerless Engineering Products Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sri Haridas Pottath is the Appellant, and Peerless Engineering Products Pvt. Ltd. alongside Dr. Sabhapathi Dorai Raju are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate governance dispute concerning the convening of an Extraordinary General Body Meeting (EOGM). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondent filed an application for the Tribunal to direct the convening of an EOGM, which the Tribunal allowed the respondents to proceed with independently. The Appellant was not the original petitioner in the matter. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT passed an order on August 29, 2017, dismissing the application for directions but giving liberty to proceed with the EOGM. The Appellant challenged this, but subsequently sought to withdraw the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant who is not the original petitioner has standing or is prejudiced by an order allowing an EOGM to proceed, such that they may challenge the order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal may be permitted to be withdrawn if the appellant is not adversely affected by the impugned order and retains the right to raise substantive issues in the appropriate corporate forum. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 186 of the Companies Act, 1956, parties can raise their grievances within the convened EOGM itself rather than preemptively litigating the procedural order to convene it. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the Appellant's non-petitioner status and confirmed that the Appellant's rights would not be compromised by attending the EOGM. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT granted the Appellant's request to withdraw the appeal, concluding that the Appellant could raise all relevant questions during the EOGM itself.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn, without any liberty to challenge the same impugned order dated August 29, 2017 before the Appellate Tribunal again. No cost.
summary: The Appellant filed an appeal against an NCLT order that allowed the Respondents to proceed with convening an Extraordinary General Body Meeting (EOGM) under Section 186 of the Companies Act, 1956. During the hearing, the NCLAT observed that the Appellant, who was not the original petitioner, would not be adversely affected by the order because he retained the right to raise all his questions and objections at the EOGM itself. Acknowledging this, the Appellant sought permission to withdraw the appeal. The NCLAT permitted the withdrawal but explicitly denied liberty to challenge the same NCLT order again, thereby dismissing the appeal without costs.

case_title: Shri Kamlesh Kalidas Shah vs Mis. Gujrat Gas Company Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shri Kamlesh Kalidas Shah is the Appellant, and Mis. Gujrat Gas Company Ltd. & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed in the brief order. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant had been pursuing the matter since 2013 before the incorrect forum. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant recognized they had been litigating in the wrong forums (erstwhile Company Law Board and then NCLT) and needed to file a civil suit for declaration. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order but subsequently requested to withdraw the appeal to file a suit for declaration accompanied by a Section 14 Limitation Act petition.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellant should be granted liberty to withdraw the appeal and pursue a suit for declaration before the appropriate forum due to prosecuting the matter before the wrong forum.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal can permit an appellant to withdraw an appeal and grant liberty to pursue remedies in the correct forum if they were previously litigating in an incorrect forum. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the Limitation Act is invoked to seek exclusion of time spent litigating bona fide in a court lacking jurisdiction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal accepted the Appellant's submission regarding their erroneous choice of forum. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT granted liberty to file the appropriate petition, subject to limitation bars, and disposed of the appeal as withdrawn.
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of as withdrawn, granting liberty to the Appellant to file a suit for declaration if otherwise not barred by limitation.
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order but subsequently requested permission to withdraw the appeal. The withdrawal was sought because the Appellant realized they had been pursuing the matter before the wrong forums (the erstwhile Company Law Board and then the NCLT) since 2013. The Appellant intended to file a suit for declaration along with a petition under Section 14 of the Limitation Act. The NCLAT granted the requested liberty, allowing the Appellant to pursue the appropriate civil remedy provided it was not barred by limitation, and disposed of the appeal as withdrawn.

case_title: Sri Trivikram & Ors vs The Mysore Stoneware Pipes & Potteries Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sri Trivikram & Ors are the Appellants/Petitioners, and The Mysore Stoneware Pipes & Potteries Ltd & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed; dispute pertains to procedural amendment of pleadings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The underlying company petition was pending for more than one year, surpassing the three-month disposal period contemplated under Section 422. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellants sought to amend their company petition specifically to enclose regulatory instructions and circulars issued by SEBI. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru rejected the application (I.A. No. 25/2016) to amend the company petition on January 3, 2017.
legal_issues: Whether a company petition must be formally amended to enclose and plead circulars issued by SEBI, RBI, or other authorities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Regulatory circulars or matters of law do not need to be formally pleaded in a petition; parties may directly rely upon them during arguments to assist the tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act requires the Tribunal to dispose of petitions expeditiously, preferably within three months. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that SEBI and RBI circulars are matters of law/regulation that are brought forth for legal assistance rather than factual pleading. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's refusal to amend the petition, confirming that the amendment was procedurally unnecessary to rely on the circulars.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without interfering with the impugned order, but the NCLT is directed to dispose of the pending company petition on its merits expeditiously, without granting unnecessary adjournments.
summary: The Appellants challenged an NCLT Bengaluru order that refused to allow an amendment to their company petition. The Appellants wanted the amendment specifically to enclose instructions and circulars issued by SEBI. The NCLAT upheld the lower tribunal's rejection, clarifying that laws or circulars from SEBI or the RBI do not need to be formally pleaded; parties can freely rely on them during hearings to assist the court. Observing that the petition had been pending for over a year, the NCLAT invoked Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013, directing the NCLT to dispose of the matter expeditiously without unnecessary adjournments.

case_title: Siddarth Jhawar & Anr vs Anurag Jhawar & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Siddarth Jhawar & Anr are the Appellants, and Anurag Jhawar & Anr are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An internal corporate dispute involving mutual allegations of oppression and mismanagement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT directed the appointment of an auditor within seven days to audit financial years 2014-15 and 2015-16. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Both parties cross-alleged mismanagement, prompting the Tribunal to order an independent valuation and audit of the company's assets. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata passed a preliminary decree on February 1, 2017, ordering the updation of accounts and a valuation audit, which the Appellants appealed to expedite the final decree.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal should expedite the final decree based on an independent auditor's report in a case of mutual allegations of oppression and mismanagement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When parties comply with a preliminary decree to appoint an independent auditor, the Tribunal must secure the auditor's report promptly and proceed to a final resolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act mandates that the Tribunal should endeavor to conclude proceedings expeditiously. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relies on the independent auditor's valuation report to resolve factual disputes regarding company assets and accounts. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since the auditor had been appointed by consensus, the focus must shift to securing the report and passing a final order uninfluenced by preliminary observations.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with directions for the auditor to submit the report early, and for the NCLT to hear the parties and pass a final order in the Company Petition expeditiously, uninfluenced by earlier observations. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellants challenged a preliminary decree issued by NCLT Kolkata regarding mutual allegations of oppression and mismanagement. The NCLT had directed the appointment of an independent auditor by consensus to update accounts and value assets for the 2014-15 and 2015-16 financial years. Noting that both parties had already complied by providing a consensus auditor's name, the NCLAT emphasized the mandate for early disposal under Section 422 of the Companies Act. The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by directing the auditor to submit an early report and ordering the NCLT to finalize the proceedings expeditiously without being swayed by preliminary observations.

case_title: Vikram Ahuja vs M/S. Greenstone Investment Pvt. Ltd. & Others
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vikram Ahuja is the Appellant, and M/s Greenstone Investment Private Limited & Others are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed; involves an ongoing dispute under a pending company petition. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original Company Petition (No. 68 of 2010) had been pending for over six years. Strict deadlines were newly imposed: amendment by Jan 31, 2017, and reply by Feb 13, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Recent developments occurred requiring an amendment to the petition, to which both parties consented. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal was filed against an unspecified NCLT Mumbai order; the NCLAT resolved the matter by consent to expedite the 6-year-old case.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellant should be permitted to amend a long-pending company petition to reflect recent developments, and how to expedite its disposal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Long-pending petitions may be amended by consent of the parties to reflect recent developments, provided strict, unextendable timelines are set for the final hearing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 expresses a legislative intent that tribunals should dispose of petitions within three months, condemning excessive pendency. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the mutual consent of the parties and the necessity created by recent developments. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT allowed the amendment by consent and imposed rigid deadlines to ensure the final disposal of the highly delayed petition.
operative_order: The Appellant is allowed to amend the Company Petition by January 31, 2017, with a reply due by February 13, 2017. NCLT Mumbai is directed to decide the petition preferably by March 31, 2017, uninfluenced by the impugned order. No cost.
summary: The Appellant challenged an order of the NCLT Mumbai Bench in a company petition that had been pending for more than six years since 2010. Given recent developments in the matter, the parties mutually consented to allow the Appellant to amend the petition. Acknowledging the extreme delay, the NCLAT invoked Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013, which aims for expedited dispute resolution. The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by setting a strict schedule: amendments by January 31, 2017, and replies by February 13, 2017, directing the NCLT to finalize the case preferably by March 31, 2017.

case_title: Valecha Engineering Ltd vs Registrar Of Companies, Mumbai
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Valecha Engineering Ltd is the Appellant, and the Registrar of Companies, Mumbai is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regulatory interactions with the Registrar of Companies; specific transaction details are not provided. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant's counsel requested withdrawal of the appeal to pursue an alternative statutory remedy for modifying the original order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an appeal against an NCLT order but subsequently opted to withdraw it to file a modification application under Section 420(2) before the NCLT.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw an appeal to seek modification of the impugned order directly from the NCLT under Section 420(2).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal may grant permission to withdraw an appeal so the appellant can pursue a statutory remedy to modify the order before the original tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 permits the NCLT to rectify or modify its own orders to correct apparent mistakes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal did not examine the merits of the case but evaluated the procedural request to withdraw. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT allowed the withdrawal without expressing any opinion on the maintainability or merits of the prospective modification petition.
operative_order: The Appellant is permitted to withdraw the appeal, and it stands disposed of as withdrawn, without any opinion expressed on the merits of the future modification petition.
summary: Valecha Engineering Ltd filed an appeal challenging an NCLT order involving the Registrar of Companies, Mumbai. During the hearing, the Appellant's counsel sought permission to withdraw the appeal. The stated intent for withdrawal was to allow the Appellant to directly approach the NCLT with an application to modify the impugned order under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLAT granted the prayer and disposed of the appeal as withdrawn, explicitly clarifying that it was not expressing any opinion on the maintainability or merits of the proposed modification petition.

case_title: Prem Sarup Narula vs Bycell Telecommunications India Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prem Sarup Narula is the Operational Creditor/Appellant, and Bycell Telecommunications India Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed, but involves operational dues claimed by the Appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Respondent claimed a sum of USD 33,000/- was already paid as a full and final settlement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A legal notice for winding up was initially issued on 24th May, 2016, and a subsequent demand notice was sent on 31st July, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor replied to the demand notice asserting that the dues were fully settled, indicating a pre-existing dispute. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi Bench dismissed the Section 9 application on 28th September, 2017, due to the existence of a dispute.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable when the corporate debtor raises a dispute regarding full and final settlement of dues.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency application by an operational creditor cannot be admitted if there is a pre-existing dispute regarding the settlement of dues. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The 'existence of dispute' under Section 9 of the IBC is satisfied when the corporate debtor provides evidence or a plausible defense of having settled the claim. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the corporate debtor's reply to the demand notice asserting full payment of USD 33,000. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since a dispute existed regarding the payment, the issue should be decided by a competent civil court and not via the corporate insolvency resolution process.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to cost.
summary: The Appellant, an Operational Creditor, challenged the NCLT's dismissal of a Section 9 IBC application against Bycell Telecommunications India Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had rejected the petition due to an existing dispute. The NCLAT upheld this decision, observing that the Corporate Debtor had replied to the statutory demand notice claiming that a sum of USD 33,000 was already paid as a full and final settlement. Consequently, the NCLAT ruled that this constituted a valid dispute that should be adjudicated by a competent civil court rather than through insolvency proceedings, dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Dilip Timblo vs Sociedade De Formento Pvt Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dilip Timblo is the Appellant, and Sociedade De Formento Pvt Ltd. & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed; involves an underlying oppression and mismanagement dispute. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original company petition was filed in 2006 and has been pending for over 11 years. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The parties confirmed that the main case was finally heard on its merits in December 2016 and judgment was reserved. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench ordered a further hearing on March 29, 2017, prompting the Appellant to challenge the delay, though they subsequently agreed not to press their interim application.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal should be directed to expedite the pronouncement of judgment in a company petition pending for 11 years that had already been fully heard.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate tribunals may direct lower tribunals to expedite the disposal of long-pending petitions where hearings have already concluded and judgments are reserved. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The lengthy pendency of 11 years for a petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 warrants expedited judicial resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed the procedural history of seven interim applications and two High Court interventions causing the 11-year delay. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Based on the parties' consensus not to press further interim applications, the NCLAT requested the NCLT to pass its final judgment expeditiously.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with a request to the President of the NCLT Principal Bench to dispose of the matter expeditiously, preferably before May 15, 2017, with no cost.
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order that scheduled further hearings for a company petition that had already been pending for over 11 years since 2006. Both parties acknowledged that the main matter had already been fully heard in December 2016 and the judgment was reserved. The Appellant agreed not to press their pending interlocutory application to avoid further delays. The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by formally requesting the NCLT Principal Bench to expedite the final disposal of the case, preferably before May 15, 2017.

case_title: P.B. Amolik & Ors vs The Bombay Diocesan Trust Association
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: P.B. Amolik & Ors are the Appellants, and The Bombay Diocesan Trust Association Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute regarding the status and election of directors and trustees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellants identified typographical errors in a previously passed judgment dated 1st May 2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants previously sought relief from the City Civil Court, Bombay, and subsequently preferred a petition that led to an earlier judgment requiring typographical correction.
legal_issues: Whether typographical errors in an earlier appellate judgment should be corrected to accurately reflect statutory provisions and party submissions.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal possesses the inherent authority to correct typographical and clerical errors in its own judgments to ensure accuracy. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 41D of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 was correctly identified to replace an erroneous reference to 'Section 22'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified the Appellant's counsel's pointings regarding drafting errors in the May 1 judgment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT ordered the rectification of three specific typographical mistakes, ensuring the judgment properly recorded the Appellants' status as elected directors rather than mere trustees.
operative_order: The judgment dated May 1, 2017, is modified to correct specific typographical errors, and a corrected copy is ordered to be issued to the parties free of cost.
summary: In this matter, the Appellants' counsel approached the NCLAT to rectify typographical errors present in a prior judgment dated May 1, 2017. The NCLAT reviewed the request and directed three specific corrections. These included replacing an incorrect reference to 'Section 22' with 'Section 41D of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950', correcting a phrase regarding the Appellants' dual status as elected Directors and Trustees, and clarifying that initial relief had been sought before the City Civil Court, Bombay. The NCLAT modified the judgment accordingly and ordered corrected copies to be distributed.

case_title: Shaw Traders vs Balaji Paper & Newsprint Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shaw Traders is the Appellant/Operational Creditor, and Balaji Paper & Newsprint Pvt. Ltd is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed; involves operational debts. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The appeal itself was filed beyond the prescribed period of limitation. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A notice of dispute was sent by the Corporate Debtor to the Operational Creditor prior to the proceedings. The Appellant repeatedly failed to appear during the hearings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority originally rejected the Section 9 application citing the Supreme Court's decision in Mobilox Innovations regarding pre-existing disputes; the subsequent appeal was adjourned on December 13 to give the Appellant a final opportunity.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal should be dismissed when it is both barred by limitation and unprosecuted due to the appellant's repeated failure to appear.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal is liable to be dismissed for default if the appellant repeatedly fails to appear, especially when the appeal is also time-barred. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC prohibits the initiation of insolvency proceedings when the corporate debtor has issued a valid notice of dispute, as interpreted by the Supreme Court in Mobilox Innovations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the physical absence of the Appellant's counsel across multiple called dates and the Registry's note regarding the expiration of limitation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that due to the persistent non-appearance and the appeal being time-barred, it warranted outright dismissal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for being barred by limitation and for default of appearance.
summary: The Appellant, an Operational Creditor, had filed a Section 9 application under the IBC which was rejected by the lower Adjudicating Authority. The rejection was based on a pre-existing dispute raised by the Corporate Debtor, relying on the Supreme Court's precedent in 'Mobilox Innovations'. When the matter reached the NCLAT, the Registry flagged the appeal as time-barred. Despite being granted an adjournment on December 13 to allow for appearance, the Appellant repeatedly failed to attend the hearings. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal for default and for being barred by limitation.

case_title: Anil Gupta & Ors vs Yogesh Mahajan & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anil Gupta & Ors are the Appellants, and Yogesh Mahajan & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not applicable; dispute centers on a procedural withdrawal. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original NCLT order in CP No 01(ND) of 2016 was passed on December 20, 2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellants claimed there was a mistake apparent on the face of the NCLT's December order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed an appeal but subsequently requested permission to withdraw it during the hearing to file a rectification application under Section 420(2) before the NCLT.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw their appeal to approach the NCLT for rectification of an order based on an alleged apparent mistake.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal may permit the withdrawal of an appeal to allow a party to pursue a statutory remedy for rectification before the lower tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420(2) of the Companies Act provides a mechanism for the NCLT to rectify its own orders if there is a mistake apparent from the record. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal did not assess the merits of the alleged mistake but accepted the procedural request to withdraw. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT allowed the withdrawal without expressing any opinion on whether a mistake actually existed on the face of the judgment.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn, enabling the Appellants to move the NCLT under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act.
summary: The Appellants filed an appeal challenging an NCLT order dated December 20, 2016. During the proceedings, their counsel submitted that there was an apparent mistake on the face of the impugned order. Consequently, the Appellants requested permission to withdraw the appeal to instead file an application under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act before the NCLT for rectification of the mistake. The NCLAT granted the request and dismissed the appeal as withdrawn, explicitly noting that it was not expressing any opinion on whether such a mistake actually existed.

case_title: Dentsu Media And Holdings India P Ltd. & Ors vs Roc Nct Of Delhi & Haryana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dentsu Media and Holdings India P Ltd. & Ors are the Appellants, and the ROC NCT of Delhi & Haryana is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regulatory matters involving the Registrar of Companies; details are not specified. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The appeal was filed with a delay of 52 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The delay in filing the appeal exceeded the maximum permissible condonation period. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed an appeal alongside a petition for condonation of delay, which was heard by the NCLAT on February 7, 2017.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal possesses the statutory authority to condone a delay in filing an appeal that exceeds the maximum limit prescribed by the Companies Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal lacks the jurisdiction to condone a delay in filing an appeal if the delay period exceeds the strict statutory maximum cap. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 restricts the Appellate Tribunal's power to condone delays to a maximum period of 45 days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal calculated the delay to be 52 days, objectively exceeding the 45-day statutory limit. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the 52-day delay surpassed the statutory maximum of 45 days, the NCLAT concluded it lacked the power to condone it, rendering the appeal barred by limitation.
operative_order: The petition for condonation of delay is dismissed. The appeal stands dismissed being barred by limitation.
summary: The Appellants, Dentsu Media and Holdings India P Ltd., filed an appeal before the NCLAT challenging an unspecified order, but the filing was delayed by 52 days. The NCLAT noted that under Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, the tribunal is statutely capped at condoning delays up to a maximum of 45 days. Because the Appellants' delay of 52 days exceeded this strict statutory limit, the NCLAT held that it had no authority to condone it. Consequently, the petition for condonation was rejected, and the appeal was dismissed as barred by limitation.

case_title: M/s Bengal Chemicals & Druggists Association vs Kalyan Choudhury
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Bengal Chemicals & Druggists Association is the Appellant, and Kalyan Choudhury is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed; involves a procedural dispute regarding limitation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The appeal was filed with a delay of 99 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant filed an application seeking to condone a 99-day delay, but repeatedly failed to appear before the Tribunal when called. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appeal and the accompanying delay condonation application were taken up by the NCLAT, resulting in a dismissal for non-prosecution.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal should be dismissed when the appellant fails to appear and prosecutes an appeal filed with a delay exceeding the statutory maximum limit.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal is liable to be dismissed for non-prosecution if the appellant consistently fails to appear before the tribunal to argue their case. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421 of the Companies Act limits the Appellate Tribunal's jurisdiction to condone delays to a strict maximum of 45 days beyond the initial 45-day filing period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the physical absence of the Appellants despite repeated calls, as well as the mathematically excessive 99-day delay. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the tribunal noted the insurmountable 99-day delay under Section 421, it ultimately concluded that the primary ground for dismissal was the Appellant's failure to prosecute the case.
operative_order: Without deliberating on the question of delay, the appeal is dismissed for non-prosecution.
summary: The Appellant, M/s Bengal Chemicals & Druggists Association, filed an appeal accompanied by an application to condone a delay of 99 days. During the hearing, the NCLAT observed that despite repeated calls, nobody appeared on behalf of the Appellant, while the Respondent's counsel was present. The NCLAT also highlighted that under Section 421 of the Companies Act, it only possesses the jurisdiction to condone a maximum delay of 45 days, making the 99-day delay statutorily unpardonable. Ultimately, without needing to formally rule on the limitation issue, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal for non-prosecution.

case_title: Devraj Vasant Immanual & Ors vs Ysp Balraj & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Devraj Vasant Immanual & Ors are the Appellants, and Ysp Balraj & Ors (including the 1st respondent company) are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allegations against the 2nd and 3rd respondents for diverting the business and siphoning off finances of the 1st respondent company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original company petition was filed in August 2016; under Section 422, it was required to be disposed of preferably within three months. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT had ordered a Chartered Accountant to investigate the 1st and 6th respondent companies on February 1, 2017, but no progress was made for over two months. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants challenged the NCLT Chennai order dated February 1, 2017, which initiated the probe but caused further delay in resolving the 9-month-old petition.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal should halt the final disposal of a company petition indefinitely to await an investigation report ordered to probe allegations of siphoning funds.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The mandate for expeditious disposal of company petitions takes precedence; tribunals should not delay final hearings indefinitely while awaiting long-pending investigation reports. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires tribunals to endeavor to dispose of petitions within three months, prohibiting unjustified, prolonged pendency. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the 9-month pendency of the case, the lack of progress in the ordered investigation over two months, and the absence of permission for time extension from the NCLT President. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that while the investigation order would not be interfered with, the main petition must proceed to final hearing with or without the report to satisfy statutory timelines.
operative_order: The Tribunal is directed to hear the parties on merit and dispose of the company petition preferably by May 15, 2017, without waiting for the investigation report. If submitted within ten days, it may be considered; otherwise, the matter proceeds on record. The appeal is disposed of.
summary: The Appellants appealed an order from NCLT Chennai that directed a Chartered Accountant to investigate allegations of financial siphoning by the respondents. The NCLAT observed that the underlying petition had been pending since August 2016, well beyond the three-month disposal preference under Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013, with no progress on the ordered investigation for over two months. Emphasizing the need for expeditious resolution, the NCLAT declined to interfere with the probe order itself but directed the NCLT to finalize the petition based on the existing record preferably by May 15, 2017, without indefinitely awaiting the investigation report.

case_title: Sysco Industries Ltd vs Ecoplast Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sysco Industries Ltd. is the Appellant, and Ecoplast Ltd. is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An insolvency dispute involving the issuance and honoring of a cheque. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Exact metrics are not detailed, but the dispute centered on underlying financial liabilities resolved via a settlement cheque. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Supreme Court disposed of the related Civil Appeal on 28th August, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The parties reached a mutual settlement during the pendency of the appeal, which included the provision of a cheque by the Appellant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Supreme Court, exercising its powers under Article 142, accepted the settlement in Civil Appeal No. 10581 of 2017, thereby closing the proceedings before the NCLT and NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal before the NCLAT should be closed when the Supreme Court has already exercised its powers under Article 142 to accept a settlement between the parties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When the Supreme Court exercises its plenary powers to accept a settlement and dispose of underlying proceedings, pending appeals before lower tribunals are rendered infructuous and must be closed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Article 142 of the Constitution of India grants the Supreme Court the authority to pass decrees necessary for doing complete justice, including validating settlements that override pending insolvency proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT solely relied on the documented order of the Supreme Court dated 28th August 2017. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Supreme Court's order explicitly disposed of the pending proceedings based on the accepted settlement, the NCLAT formally closed the appeal before it.
operative_order: In view of the order passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the appeal is closed and stands disposed of.
summary: In this insolvency appeal between Sysco Industries Ltd and Ecoplast Ltd, the NCLAT was informed that the parties had reached a mutual settlement. The Supreme Court of India had already reviewed this matter in Civil Appeal No. 10581 of 2017. Exercising its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court accepted the settlement on August 28, 2017, directing that the provided cheque must be honored to avoid contempt, and subsequently disposed of the pending NCLT proceedings. Bound by the Supreme Court's order disposing of the underlying matter, the NCLAT officially closed and disposed of the present appeal.

case_title: Srei Infrastructure Finance Ltd vs Naveen Bansal & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Respondent No. 1 (Naveen Bansal) is the Petitioner; Appellant (SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd) is the Financier (5th Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant financed approximately Rs. 50 crores to the company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; dispute centers on corporate oppression. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable as it is governed by Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act 1956. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant filed an interim application stating there was a privity of contract between the parties, which it later alleged was a typographical error. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Company Petition No.99/2014 was filed alleging oppression and mismanagement. The Appellant sought dismissal of the petition against it, which the NCLT rejected on May 17, 2017. The Appellant subsequently sought to withdraw its appeal to rectify the typographical error before the NCLT.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant should be permitted to withdraw its appeal to rectify an alleged typographical error in its pleadings before the lower Tribunal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will permit the withdrawal of an appeal to allow a party to rectify erroneous pleadings before the lower adjudicating authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: N/A. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The tribunal allowed the withdrawal without determining the merit of whether the pleading was genuinely a typographical error, leaving it to the lower tribunal.
