operative_order: The appeal is disposed of as withdrawn with no order as to cost. The Tribunal may consider the application uninfluenced by the Appellate Tribunal's observations if the issue is raised again.
summary: The respondent filed a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement against the company, impleading the appellant financier. The appellant sought dismissal of the petition against it, which the NCLT rejected based on the appellant's own pleading of a privity of contract. Claiming this was a typographical error, the appellant sought to withdraw its appeal to correct the error before the NCLT. The NCLAT allowed the withdrawal without ruling on the merits.

case_title: Axis Nirman And Industries Limited & Anr vs M/S. Hotel Birsa (P) Limited & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/S. Hotel Birsa (P) Limited & Ors are the Petitioners; Axis Nirman and Industries Limited is Appellant 1 (Respondent No. 7 below). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute regarding internal shareholding, unauthorized increase in share capital, and a Memorandum of Understanding to sell shares to an external entity, Libra Retailer Private Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Disputed share allotments of 1,20,000 and 90,000 shares to Respondents 7 and 4 respectively. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A petition was filed alleging oppression and mismanagement. On April 7, 2017, the NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed the petition, cancelled specific share allotments, and directed the petitioners to execute share transfers to an outsider (Libra). The Appellants challenged this common order.
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal adjudicating an oppression and mismanagement petition has the jurisdiction to direct the sale of shares to an outsider when other existing shareholders are present.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Company Law Tribunal lacks the jurisdiction to compel the sale of a party's shares to an outsider, particularly when existing shareholders might be willing to purchase them. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Remedial directives under the Companies Act cannot mandatorily enforce an MoU favoring a non-member outsider against internal shareholder rights. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: N/A. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While affirming the finding of oppression and mismanagement, the NCLAT concluded that directing the sale of shares to an external party exceeded the Tribunal's jurisdiction.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed in part, setting aside the NCLT's direction that compelled the sale of shares to the outsider entity, in alignment with a parallel judgment (C.A (AT) No. 162 of 2017). No order as to cost.
summary: In an oppression and mismanagement petition, the NCLT Kolkata allowed the petition, cancelled various share allotments, and uniquely directed the petitioners to sell their shares to an outsider entity under a Memorandum of Understanding. The appellants challenged this order. Relying on its precedent in a connected appeal, the NCLAT ruled that the NCLT lacked jurisdiction to mandate the sale of shares to an outsider when existing shareholders were available. It set aside that specific direction while upholding the core finding of oppression and mismanagement.

case_title: Vimal Organics Limited vs Anya Polytech & Fertilizers Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vimal Organics Limited is the Operational Creditor; Anya Polytech & Fertilizers Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A May 3, 2014 agreement for the supply, engineering, erection, and commissioning of a 50MTPD Zinc Sulphate Manufacturing Plant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid invoices related to the supply of goods and services (amount unstated). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice was issued; Corporate Debtor replied on July 20, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Emails dated February 25, May 31, and June 18, 2016, wherein the Corporate Debtor raised prior complaints regarding improper commissioning, failure to achieve the 40.0 MT/day production target, and 15 undelivered items. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 IBC petition, which NCLT New Delhi dismissed on October 10, 2017, due to a pre-existing dispute.
legal_issues: Whether the complaints regarding improper commissioning, design defects, and failure to meet production targets raised prior to the demand notice constitute a pre-existing 'dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for corporate insolvency resolution by an operational creditor is not maintainable if there is a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding the quality or performance of the supplied goods or services. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Existence of a dispute' under Section 5(6) read with Section 9 encompasses contemporaneous correspondence highlighting defective performance prior to the Section 8 demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Emails exchanged before the issuance of the demand notice evidencing non-performance and failure to achieve production targets successfully establish a valid pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found that the evidence clearly demonstrated a pre-existing dispute regarding commissioning and plant performance, thereby barring the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed due to the existence of a pre-existing dispute. No cost.
summary: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 IBC petition for unpaid invoices related to a Zinc Sulphate plant. The NCLT dismissed the petition, citing a pre-existing dispute. On appeal, the NCLAT upheld the dismissal, observing that emails sent by the Corporate Debtor prior to the Section 8 demand notice clearly evidenced a pre-existing dispute regarding defective design, improper commissioning, undelivered items, and failure to meet production targets.

case_title: Steamline Industries Ltd vs Tecpro Systems Ltd. & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Steamline Industries Ltd. is the Appellant/Plaintiff; Tecpro Systems Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited is the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Civil commercial claim underlying Civil Suit (COMM) 123/2017 pending before the Delhi High Court. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The initiation of CIRP against the Corporate Debtor by Edelweiss in Company Petition No. (IB) 197(PB)/2017 and the subsequent declaration of a Section 14 moratorium. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Seeking to continue its pending suit in the Delhi High Court under the Commercial Courts Act, the Appellant filed an application before the NCLT Principal Bench. The NCLT rejected the application on October 9, 2017, citing the statutory moratorium.
legal_issues: Whether a civil suit filed under the Commercial Courts Act can proceed against a Corporate Debtor despite the imposition of a moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC imposes a complete bar on the continuation of any pending civil suits against a corporate debtor, overriding conflicting laws. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 238 of the IBC, the Code has an overriding effect over any inconsistent provisions in other laws, nullifying the Appellant's argument that the Commercial Courts Act should prevail. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The mere existence of an active CIRP and Section 14 moratorium automatically triggers the statutory bar on parallel proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the suit cannot proceed due to the overriding nature of Section 238 and the strict mandate of Section 14, thereby affirming the NCLT's refusal to grant leave.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The Appellant is granted liberty to file its claim before the Insolvency Resolution Professional for consideration along with other claimants in accordance with the law. No separate cost.
summary: Following the initiation of CIRP against Tecpro Systems Ltd., the Appellant sought permission to continue its pending civil suit in the Delhi High Court. The NCLT rejected this request citing the Section 14 moratorium. The Appellant argued that the Commercial Courts Act should prevail over the IBC. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 238 of the IBC grants it overriding effect over other laws, thus strictly barring the continuation of the suit. The Appellant was permitted to submit its claim to the Resolution Professional.

case_title: Northern Projects Ltd. & Ors. vs Blue Coast Hotels & Resorts Ltd. & Others
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 401 of 2017 (with Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 404 to 408 of 2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Northern Projects Ltd. & Ors. are the Appellants; Blue Coast Hotels & Resorts Ltd. & Others are the Respondents (with Respondents 2 to 5 being the affected shareholders). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proceedings concerning the rectification of entries in the register of members regarding equity shares held by Respondents 2 to 5, alongside a proposed extension of the redemption period of preference shares by postal ballot. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Corporate membership and shareholding dispute). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Erstwhile Company Law Board (CLB) interim order passed on August 11, 2011; impugned NCLT order passed on September 19, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CLB order of August 11, 2011, restraining Respondents 2 to 5 from exercising voting rights; and the proposed resolution under Section 48 of the Companies Act 2013 to extend preference share redemption. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Originating from T.C.P. Nos. 9 to 14/111A/NCLT/MB/MAH/2011 before the NCLT Mumbai Bench. Respondents 3 to 5 moved an interlocutory application seeking modification of the CLB interim order, but the NCLT rejected the modification while erroneously reciting the reliefs sought in the main Company Petition rather than the application.
legal_issues: Whether an order passed on an interlocutory application that suffers from ambiguity and erroneously recites the substantive prayers of the main company petition can be sustained.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicating tribunal must clearly identify the specific application before it and cannot adjudicate an interlocutory application by reciting and addressing the substantive reliefs reserved for the main petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Procedural propriety under the Companies Act mandates that prayers for modifying interim arrangements must be evaluated distinctly from the final remedies claimed under Section 111A or voting rights under Section 48. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Patent ambiguity on the record, conceded by opposing counsel, regarding which application was actually being decided invalidates the resulting order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the lower tribunal conflated the interim application with the main company petition, the resulting order was defective and required remand for joint disposal on the merits.
operative_order: The impugned order dated September 19, 2017, is set aside. The matter is remitted to the NCLT Mumbai Bench to decide the main Company Petition(s) along with all pending Interlocutory Application(s) together on merit after notice and hearing the parties, preferably within two months. The appeal is allowed with no order as to costs.
summary: The appellants appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order refusing to modify an interim CLB order restraining certain respondents from exercising voting rights. The NCLAT observed a patent ambiguity on the face of the impugned order, as the lower Tribunal had adjudicated an interlocutory application but erroneously extracted and recited the substantive reliefs claimed in the main company petition. With the respondents conceding the mistake, the NCLAT held that the ambiguous order could not stand. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the order, and remitted the matter to the NCLT to decide the company petitions and all pending interlocutory applications jointly on merits within two months.

case_title: M/s. Oxygen Communications & Anr. vs M/s. Iris Computers Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Oxygen Communications & Anr. is the Operational Creditor; M/s. Iris Computers Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational transaction resulting in a claimed debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified debt amount. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant issued notices on March 23 and April 20, 2017; the Respondent disputed the amount on May 30, 2017; a Section 8 demand notice was issued on August 8, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Prior correspondence on May 30, 2017 demonstrating a dispute, and a Section 8 notice sent by an Advocate/Solicitor firm rather than the operational creditor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi dismissed the Section 9 application on September 27, 2017, citing a pre-existing dispute.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 is maintainable if there is a pre-existing dispute and the statutory demand notice under Section 8(1) is issued by an advocate rather than the operational creditor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor's insolvency petition is not maintainable if a dispute regarding the debt existed prior to the statutory demand notice, or if the notice is improperly issued by a legal firm instead of the creditor itself. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(1) of the IBC requires the demand notice to be delivered by the Operational Creditor; issuance by an advocate is impermissible. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented disputes occurring before the Section 8 notice date establish a valid pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal because a pre-existing dispute was proven and the demand notice was technically defective.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to cost.
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC petition. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal on two distinct grounds: first, prior correspondence showed the Corporate Debtor had disputed the debt before the Section 8 notice was issued, establishing a pre-existing dispute. Second, relying on precedent, the NCLAT held that the Section 8 demand notice was invalid because it was issued by a law firm rather than the Operational Creditor itself. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: M/s. Custodial Services (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs M/s. Metaflims (India) Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Custodial Services (India) Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant; M/s. Metaflims (India) Ltd. is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: N/A. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT order passed on July 13, 2017; initial 45-day deadline was August 27, 2017; absolute maximum condonable limit (+45 days) expired on October 12, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The appeal was initially presented with defects on October 11, 2017, taken back, and finally filed on October 23, 2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai passed an order under the IBC on July 13, 2017. The Appellant filed an appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act on October 23, 2017, with a petition to condone the delay.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can condone a filing delay beyond the maximum 45-day extension limit provided by statute, and whether an IBC order can be appealed under the Companies Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Appellate Tribunal lacks jurisdiction to condone filing delays beyond the strict statutory maximum limit, and appeals must be filed under the specific statute governing the original proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421(3) of the Companies Act caps the condonable delay at exactly 45 days beyond the standard filing period; furthermore, IBC matters are strictly appealable under Section 61 IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mechanical calculation of days from the order date to the definitive filing date. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was rejected for being fatally time-barred beyond the tribunal's condonation powers and for being filed under an incorrect statutory provision.
operative_order: The petition for condonation of delay is rejected, and the appeal is dismissed as barred by limitation and not maintainable. No cost.
summary: The appellant challenged an NCLT order passed under the IBC by filing an appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, significantly past the deadline. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal on two grounds: first, it lacked jurisdiction to condone a delay that exceeded the maximum 45-day extension permitted by statute. Second, the appeal was procedurally defective because orders passed under the IBC must be appealed under Section 61 of the IBC, not the Companies Act.

case_title: State Bank of India vs S. Muthuraju & 3 others
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India is the Appellant (Financial Creditor); S. Muthuraju (former IRP) and others are Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying corporate debt involving SARFAESI enforcement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The original IRP (Muthuraju) was replaced by a new Resolution Professional who assumed control. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai directed SBI to hand over physical possession of corporate debtor assets to the IRP within two days or face action under Section 74 of the IBC. SBI appealed. Subsequently, respondents filed a fresh application before the NCLT seeking action for violation of the earlier order.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal challenging directions to hand over asset possession to a specific IRP becomes infructuous upon the replacement of that IRP and the filing of fresh proceedings before the lower tribunal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interlocutory appeal becomes infructuous when the factual matrix fundamentally changes (e.g., replacement of the key official) and identical issues are being actively pursued in a fresh application before the adjudicating authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: N/A. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that because a new RP had taken over and a fresh application was pending before the NCLT regarding the same issue, nothing survived for consideration in the present appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is treated as infructuous and stands disposed of. The appellant is permitted to pursue its remedies before the NCLT.
summary: The NCLT directed the State Bank of India to hand over physical possession of the Corporate Debtor's assets to the IRP or face penal action under Section 74 of the IBC. SBI appealed this directive. During the appeal process, the original IRP was replaced by a new Resolution Professional, and a fresh application regarding the possession issue was filed before the NCLT. Consequently, the NCLAT ruled that nothing survived for consideration, disposing of the appeal as infructuous and directing SBI to pursue remedies before the NCLT.

case_title: Erofab Exports Private Limited & Ors vs Gartex Insta Apparels Private Limited & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Erofab Exports Pvt Ltd & Ors are the Appellants/Petitioners; Gartex Insta Apparels Pvt Ltd & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over internal company management, 50% shareholding, and board appointments. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Bengaluru order passed on September 14, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants claimed respondents filed fictitious AOC-4 and MGT-7 forms with the ROC. Respondents claimed Petitioners 2 and 3 ceased to be directors under an MoU. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru rejected the Appellants' interim application seeking to freeze corporate actions and block ROC filings. The Appellants challenged this refusal of interim relief.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal should interfere with an interlocutory order denying interim relief when the main company petition remains pending for final adjudication.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will generally decline to interfere with interlocutory orders denying interim relief if the underlying main petition can be expedited for final disposal on merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act 2013 encourages the expeditious disposal of proceedings by tribunals. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: N/A. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT chose not to evaluate the merits of the interim relief claim, instead directing the NCLT to finalize the substantive proceedings swiftly.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without interfering with the NCLT's interim order. The NCLT is expected to decide the main Company Petition within two months uninfluenced by the interim order, without granting unnecessary adjournments. No costs.
summary: The appellants challenged an NCLT order that denied their request for interim relief to restrain respondents from making allegedly fraudulent regulatory filings and undertaking coercive corporate actions. The NCLAT declined to interfere with the NCLT's interlocutory decision or evaluate the competing claims regarding shareholding and board appointments. Emphasizing the need for timely resolution, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal by directing the NCLT to decide the main petition on its merits within two months.

case_title: State Bank of India vs S. Muthuraju & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Financial Creditor) is Appellant; S. Muthuraju (IRP) & Ors are Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim of financial debt and enforcement actions under the SARFAESI Act. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT order passed on July 7, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The IRP initially allegedly refused to recognize SBI as a financial creditor. SBI had possession of corporate debtor land under SARFAESI. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT directed SBI to cooperate with the IRP and hand over possession of assets under its control. SBI appealed this direction.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an IRP has adjudicatory authority to decide who qualifies as a creditor. 2. Whether a financial creditor holding assets under the SARFAESI Act must surrender possession to the IRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Interim Resolution Professional lacks the adjudicatory power to definitively reject creditor status; disputes over the mandatory surrender of assets possessed under other statutes must be decided by the Adjudicating Authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The IRP's role is to verify claims, not adjudicate creditor status. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: N/A. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the IRP conceded to treat SBI as a creditor subject to verification, SBI was allowed to join the CoC. The NCLAT left the SARFAESI possession issue open for the NCLT to determine.
operative_order: SBI is permitted to take part in the CoC meetings. The issue of whether a Financial Creditor must hand over SARFAESI-possessed land is left open to be decided by the Adjudicating Authority if raised. The appeal stands disposed of.
summary: The State Bank of India appealed an NCLT order directing it to cooperate with the IRP and surrender possession of the Corporate Debtor's assets. SBI contended that the IRP was illegitimately refusing to recognize it as a financial creditor. The NCLAT noted that an IRP prima facie lacks adjudicatory power to reject creditor status, and based on the IRP's undertaking, allowed SBI to participate in the Committee of Creditors. The question of whether SBI must surrender assets held under the SARFAESI Act was left to be decided by the NCLT.

case_title: PCK Buderus (India) Special Steels Pvt. Ltd. vs Sungil India Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: PCK Buderus (India) Special Steels Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor (Appellant); Sungil India Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational debt (specifics unstated). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT order was passed on November 3, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The statutory Section 8 demand notice was issued by an advocate who did not hold any position with or in relation to the operational creditor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed the insolvency petition, holding the Section 8 notice suffered from an incurable technical defect. The Appellant challenged this dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 8 demand notice issued by an independent advocate, who holds no position within the operational creditor's organization, is legally valid under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory demand notice under the IBC must be issued by the operational creditor itself or an authorized person holding a position with or in relation to the operational creditor; an independent advocate cannot validly issue it. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict compliance with Section 8 of the IBC dictates that the issuer must have a structural relationship with the operational creditor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: If the issuer is solely an external advocate lacking any internal position in the creditor company, the notice is inherently defective. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Relying on its Macquarie Bank precedent, the NCLAT affirmed that the advocate's notice was incurably defective, rendering the insolvency application unmaintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. However, the Appellant is granted liberty to initiate a fresh process after complying with the mandate of law.
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed the NCLT's dismissal of its insolvency application. The NCLT had rejected the petition because the Section 8 demand notice was issued by an external advocate rather than the creditor itself. Relying on its precedent in Macquarie Bank, the NCLAT affirmed that a statutory demand notice issued by a lawyer who holds no position with the operational creditor is inherently and incurably defective under the IBC. The appeal was dismissed with liberty granted to initiate a fresh legal process.

case_title: United Motors Heavy Equipment Pvt. Ltd vs Sundaram Industries Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: United Motors Heavy Equipment Pvt. Ltd is the Operational Creditor; Sundaram Industries Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of 30 solid tyres by the appellant through the Corporate Debtor to a third-party end user. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT order was passed on June 15, 2017; the pivotal dispute email was dated November 15, 2011. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: An e-mail dated November 15, 2011, demonstrated that the engineering department of the end-user raised objections regarding the substandard quality of the tyres. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected the Section 9 application citing the existence of a pre-existing dispute based on the Kirusa Software precedent. The appellant challenged this rejection.
legal_issues: Whether a historical email raising quality objections constitutes a valid pre-existing 'dispute' barring a Section 9 application under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor's insolvency petition is not maintainable if there is documented evidence of a pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of the goods supplied. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Existence of dispute' under the IBC encompasses substantive, prior complaints about substandard materials. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented historical complaints from the end-user regarding product quality successfully establish a genuine pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found the 2011 email sufficient to establish a pre-existing dispute, thereby affirming the NCLT's rejection of the petition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no costs. The dismissal does not prejudice the appellant's right to pursue its pending civil suit before a competent court.
summary: The Operational Creditor challenged the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 9 insolvency petition. The NCLT had rejected it due to a pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of 30 solid tyres supplied. The Corporate Debtor produced a 2011 email demonstrating that the end-user had complained about substandard materials. The NCLAT held that this email clearly established a pre-existing 'existence of dispute' prior to the Section 8 notice, rendering the Section 9 application non-maintainable. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mayur Rastogi vs Registrar Of Companies
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mayur Rastogi (and Manav Rastogi in the connected appeal) are the Appellants; the Registrar of Companies is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: N/A (Regulatory compliance). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Imposition of a Rs. 1,00,000 fine for a compliance default that continued for approximately 9 years. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The dual DINs were originally applied for in 2006. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The appellants concurrently held two Director Identification Numbers (DINs) for 9 years, allegedly due to initial computerization confusion. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellants filed compounding applications before the NCLT. The NCLT compounded the offence but imposed a fine of Rs. 1,00,000 each. The appellants appealed, seeking a reduction of the fine.
legal_issues: Whether a fine of Rs. 1,00,000 for holding two DINs for 9 years is excessive and warrants reduction, and whether an appeal is maintainable against an order compounding an offence on the appellant's own application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Holding multiple Director Identification Numbers is a serious statutory violation affecting economic integrity, and long-standing defaults cannot be excused by citing initial administrative or technological confusion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The prohibition against multiple DINs under Section 266C (1956 Act) / Section 155 (2013 Act) is strict to prevent corporate fraud. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Holding a dual DIN for an extended 9-year period constitutes a severe non-compliance that justifies a substantial compounding fine. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the fine was justified given the length and severity of the default, and additionally questioned the legal maintainability of appealing a compounding order.
operative_order: Both appeals are rejected.
summary: The appellants challenged an NCLT order that imposed a fine of Rs. 1,00,000 each for compounding their offence of holding two Director Identification Numbers (DINs) for nearly 9 years. They argued the dual DINs were an inadvertent mistake caused by confusion during the 2006 computerization process. The NCLAT rejected this defense, emphasizing that holding two DINs for an extended period is a serious economic violation. Finding the fine justified and questioning the appeal's maintainability against a compounding order, the NCLAT dismissed the appeals.

case_title: City Hospital Pvt. Ltd & Anr vs Mohan Paul & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: City Hospital Pvt. Ltd & Anr are the Appellants; Mohan Paul & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over the issuance and internal transfer of 45 equity shares. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Imposition of Rs. 50,000 in costs by the lower tribunal. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT order was passed on June 7, 2017; the NCLAT issued an interim stay on costs on July 12, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant demonstrated full compliance with the substantive directive of the Tribunal by issuing the 45 shares to the Respondent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT allowed the Respondent's petition regarding the shares and imposed a Rs. 50,000 cost on the Appellant. The Appellant filed a limited appeal solely challenging the imposition of costs.
legal_issues: Whether a punitive cost imposed by a tribunal should be sustained when the appellant has fully and bona fide complied with the substantive directives of the impugned order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal may exercise discretion to waive punitive costs imposed by a lower adjudicating authority if the penalized party demonstrates prompt and full compliance with the substantive relief ordered. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Concrete proof of compliance with the primary directive (issuing the shares) justifies removing the secondary cost penalty, especially when the opposing party concedes. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appellant complied with the order to issue the shares in letter and spirit, the NCLAT deemed the imposition of costs unnecessary.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed in part. The substantive order of the NCLT is affirmed, but the final portion imposing a cost of Rs. 50,000 on the appellant is set aside.
summary: The NCLT allowed a shareholder's petition directing the issuance of 45 equity shares and imposed a cost of Rs. 50,000 on the appellant company. The company filed a limited appeal challenging only the imposition of the costs. The NCLAT observed that the company had already complied with the substantive portion of the NCLT's order in letter and spirit by successfully issuing the shares. With the respondent raising no objection to the cost waiver, the NCLAT allowed the appeal in part, setting aside the Rs. 50,000 cost while affirming the rest of the order.

case_title: M/S Aggcon International Equipments Pvt. Ltd. vs Isolux Corsan India Engineering and Construction Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Aggcon International Equipments Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor (Appellant); Isolux Corsan India Engineering and Construction Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An underlying operational agreement executed with a joint venture firm named 'Isolux Corsan India-C&C JV'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT order was passed on July 21, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The actual agreement was executed with the JV firm, which is not a company incorporated under the Companies Act, and the JV firm was not made a party to the application. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh dismissed the Section 9 IBC application because the claim was filed against the corporate Respondent rather than the actual contracting JV firm. The Appellant challenged this dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether an insolvency application is maintainable against a specific corporate entity when the underlying operational agreement was strictly with an unincorporated joint venture firm involving that entity.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency petition cannot be maintained against a specific corporate entity if the actual contractual privity and operational debt lie against a separate, unincorporated joint venture. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC requires strict privity of contract with the specific 'Corporate Debtor' named in the petition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: If the foundational operational agreement names a joint venture (which is not a registered company) rather than the respondent company, the petition fails for lack of privity and misjoinder. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed that because the agreement was with the JV and not the Respondent company, the Section 9 application against the Respondent was legally unmaintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no cost. No interference with the NCLT's impugned order is called for.
summary: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 IBC application against the Respondent company. The NCLT dismissed it, noting that the actual agreement and subsequent claim were against an unincorporated joint venture firm ('Isolux Corsan India-C&C JV'), not the Respondent company itself, and the JV was not impleaded. The NCLAT affirmed this dismissal, holding that since contractual privity existed strictly with the joint venture rather than the specific corporate entity, the insolvency application against the Respondent was not maintainable.

case_title: IL&FS Transport Networks Ltd. vs Regional Airport Holding International Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: IL&FS Transport Networks Ltd. is the Appellant; Regional Airport Holding International Ltd. & Ors. are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allegations of corporate oppression and mismanagement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The underlying company petition was pending for five years. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant sought to introduce subsequent facts via an additional affidavit and implead the company's directors, alleging collusion. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT allowed the additional affidavit but the Appellant appealed, pressing for the formal impleadment of the directors and amendment of pleadings at the final hearing stage.
legal_issues: Whether a petitioner can amend pleadings and implead non-member directors in an oppression and mismanagement petition five years after its filing, at the stage of final hearing.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Delayed applications to implead non-members and amend pleadings at the final hearing stage of a long-pending oppression petition are impermissible, especially when the tribunal already possesses inherent powers to address proven oppression. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 grants the Tribunal sweeping powers to pass any order 'as it deems fit and proper' if oppression is found, rendering late-stage pleading amendments unnecessary. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Possessing knowledge of alleged facts for five years without acting upon them bars a late impleadment application. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT rejected the amendment and impleadment due to the extreme delay and the sufficiency of the Tribunal's statutory powers under Section 242.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no cost. The Appellant is permitted to file its additional affidavit by October 3, 2017, and parties are directed to cooperate for the early disposal of the case.
summary: The appellant challenged an NCLT order to press for the impleadment of company directors and the amendment of pleadings in a five-year-old oppression and mismanagement petition. The NCLAT noted that the appellant had prior knowledge of these facts but severely delayed the application. The tribunal held that since the targeted individuals were not members of the company and the petition was already at the final hearing stage, the amendment was procedurally unwarranted. Furthermore, Section 242(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, grants the Tribunal sufficient inherent power to pass necessary orders if oppression is conclusively proven. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Prime Cars Pvt. Ltd. vs Reliance Commercial Finance Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prime Cars Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant (Corporate Debtor); Reliance Commercial Finance Ltd. is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Ahmedabad initiated CIRP on September 4, 2017; Settlement Deed executed on September 30, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The parties executed a Settlement Deed, and the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) was paid as per the settlement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad initiated ex-parte CIRP against the Appellant. The Appellant appealed, secured an interim order, and settled the dispute. The Supreme Court subsequently set aside the NCLAT's interim order and disposed of the matter under Article 142.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT should formally close an underlying insolvency petition after the Supreme Court, exercising its Article 142 powers based on a settlement deed, sets aside the interim appellate proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate debtor must be freed from the rigors of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process when the Supreme Court exercises its inherent constitutional powers to dispose of the matter based on a mutual settlement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A (Ruling predicated on Article 142 of the Constitution). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The explicit directive of the Supreme Court order combined with confirmation that the IRP's fees were settled. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Recognizing the Supreme Court's overriding order and the factual settlement of dues, the NCLAT formally directed the Adjudicating Authority to close the insolvency petition.
operative_order: The Adjudicating Authority is directed to close C.P.(I.B.) No. 87/7/NCLT/AHM/2017. The appellant company is freed from the CIRP. No cost.
summary: The corporate debtor appealed an ex-parte NCLT order initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under the IBC. During the pendency of the appellate proceedings, the parties successfully reached a mutual settlement and subsequently approached the Supreme Court. Exercising its inherent jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court took the Settlement Deed on record and explicitly set aside the impugned interim orders, effectively disposing of the pending NCLAT matter. Acknowledging the Supreme Court's directive and confirming that the Interim Resolution Professional had been compensated, the NCLAT formally directed the Adjudicating Authority to close the underlying insolvency petition.

case_title: Sanjay Agarwal & Ors. vs M/s Meghalaya Finleaase Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sanjay Agarwal & Ors. are Appellants/Petitioners; M/s Meghalaya Finleaase Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. are Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint operation of a business and internal share transfers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Share transfers executed in 2014; Annual Return filed on September 30, 2014. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The 2014 Annual Return showed the 1st petitioner held 42.55%, the 2nd respondent held 40.80%, and an outsider held 8.28%. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed an oppression petition alleging the 8.28% outsider shares should have been transferred to the 2nd respondent. NCLT New Delhi dismissed the petition for delay, laches, estoppel, and acquiescence. Appellants challenged this dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether the failure of a company to transfer a minority block of an outsider's shares to a respondent constitutes oppression or mismanagement against the petitioning shareholders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The mere failure to transfer a minority block of shares from an external party to a respondent does not inherently constitute actionable oppression or mismanagement against the petitioning shareholders or the company. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: To warrant relief under Section 402 (1956 Act) or Section 242 (2013 Act), the impugned conduct must demonstrably oppress the petitioners or mismanage the company's affairs, which was absent here. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The petitioners failed to demonstrate how the retention of shares by an outsider prejudicially affected their own rights. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Bypassing the issue of delay, the NCLAT concluded on merits that the factual grievance did not meet the legal threshold for oppression or mismanagement.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed on merits with no order as to costs.
summary: The appellants challenged an NCLT order that dismissed their oppression and mismanagement petition on initial grounds of delay, laches, estoppel, and acquiescence. Electing to hear the matter on its substantive merits, the NCLAT observed that the appellants' core grievance was the alleged mala fide failure to transfer an outsider's 8.28% shareholding directly to the second respondent. The NCLAT definitively ruled that this specific non-transfer did not constitute actionable oppression or mismanagement qua the petitioning shareholders or the company itself. Concluding that no statutory relief could be granted under the Companies Act on these specific facts, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Malaxmi Infra Ventures (India) Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs Brahmani Infratech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Malaxmi Infra Ventures (India) Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. are the Appellants; Brahmani Infratech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: N/A (Internal corporate management). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The 1st petitioner was admitted as a shareholder on March 21, 2011; NCLT Hyderabad passed its order on January 31, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: N/A. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad held the oppression petition maintainable only for the 1st petitioner and not the 2nd, while directing the 2nd appellant to continue as a director. The Appellants sought to withdraw the appeal to file a fresh petition. The Respondents objected to the directorship directive, noting they had filed a cross-appeal (No. 89 of 2017).
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw an appeal regarding maintainability to file a fresh petition, while deferring a contested interim directive regarding a directorship to a separate cross-appeal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will permit the withdrawal of an appeal with liberty to file a fresh petition based on a correct cause of action, without prejudicing the adjudication of connected cross-appeals. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Petitions under Sections 241 and 242 require the petitioner to establish oppression occurring strictly after they legally acquired shareholder status. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: N/A. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT permitted the withdrawal for filing a fresh petition but explicitly declined to validate the lower tribunal's order allowing the 2nd appellant to continue as a director, deferring that matter to the parallel appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of as withdrawn. The Appellants are granted liberty to file a fresh petition under Sections 241/242 for oppression occurring after they became shareholders. The Tribunal shall decide any future petition uninfluenced by prior orders.
summary: The appellants challenged an NCLT order which ruled their oppression petition maintainable only for the first petitioner, while simultaneously directing the second petitioner to continue functioning as a director. During the appellate hearing, the appellants requested permission to withdraw the appeal to file a fresh petition regarding oppression occurring specifically after they acquired their shareholder status. The respondents strongly objected to the directorship continuation, noting they had already filed a separate cross-appeal against that specific directive. The NCLAT permitted the withdrawal with liberty to file a fresh petition, expressly leaving the fiercely contested directorship issue to be resolved in the parallel cross-appeal.

case_title: Shri Kamlesh Kalidas Shah vs Asian Paints (India) Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shri Kamlesh Kalidas Shah is the Appellant; Asian Paints (India) Ltd & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Transfer of corporate shares. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The instrument for share transfer was submitted 24 years after its execution. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The respondent company rejected the transfer because the transferor's signature on the instrument did not tally with the company's specimen signature records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai dismissed the Appellant's petition under Section 58(4) because the disputed signature rendered the instrument improper under Section 56, and directed the Appellant to a civil court. The Appellant challenged this dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether a Company Law Tribunal has the summary jurisdiction to compel a company to register a share transfer when the company bona fide disputes the authenticity of the transferor's signature.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Company Law Tribunal cannot compel the registration of a share transfer if there is a bona fide dispute regarding the authenticity of the transferor's signature; such evidentiary disputes must be adjudicated by a civil court. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 56 of the Companies Act, an instrument bearing a mismatched or disputed signature ceases to be a 'proper instrument of transfer,' precluding the Tribunal from issuing a mandatory direction under Section 58(4). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A clear mismatch between the submitted signature and the company's specimen records is sufficient to oust the summary jurisdiction of the Tribunal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed that the appellant must prove rightful ownership and the validity of the signature in a civil court, thereby dismissing the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no cost. The Appellant is granted liberty to seek appropriate remedy before a civil court.
summary: The appellant sought to register a share transfer instrument a remarkable 24 years after its initial execution. The respondent company rejected the transfer request because the transferor's signature on the document did not match its official specimen records. The NCLT dismissed the appellant's subsequent petition, ruling that an instrument bearing a disputed signature is not a valid or "proper instrument" under Section 56 of the Companies Act. The tribunal emphasized that such complex evidentiary disputes strictly require civil court adjudication. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, agreeing that the appellant must establish rightful ownership and signature validity before a civil court, ultimately dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Digha Seafood Exports Pvt. Ltd. & Ors vs Ram Milan Singh & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Digha Seafood Exports Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant No. 1), Prabhat Kumar (Appellant No. 2), and another (Appellant No. 3). Respondent No. 1 is Ram Milan Singh. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over shareholding and directorship in the Appellant No. 1 Company, alongside personal guarantees to Canara Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; dispute was regarding shares and management, not a debt default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A joint petition with agreed terms of settlement dated 2017-08-09 was produced, signed by directors and witnesses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appeal was filed to resolve disputes over share transfer and directorship.
legal_issues: Whether the appellate tribunal should record the compromise and dispose of the appeal based on the joint settlement terms filed by the parties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal may be disposed of in terms of a mutually agreed settlement filed jointly by the parties. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal verified the signatures of the authorized representatives and witnesses on the joint settlement terms. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The tribunal concluded that the settlement was valid and bound the parties, thus disposing of the appeal on those terms.
operative_order: The joint terms of settlement are accepted and kept on record. The appeal is disposed of in terms of the settlement, treating the terms as a binding direction of the Appellate Tribunal. Parties allowed to file fees within two weeks. No costs.
summary: In this matter between Digha Seafood Exports Pvt. Ltd. and Ram Milan Singh, the parties reached an amicable resolution regarding their dispute over shareholding and directorship. The agreed terms stipulated the transfer of 3,09,247 shares (37%) for Rs. 64,94,187 to Respondent No. 1, his reinstatement as a Director, and his provision of a personal guarantee to Canara Bank. The NCLAT accepted the joint petition and the agreed terms of settlement dated August 9, 2017. Consequently, the tribunal disposed of the appeal, making the settlement terms binding on all signatories, with no order as to costs.

case_title: Vinod Kumar Kapoor vs Vijay Khanna & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vinod Kumar Kapoor (Contemnor No. 2, Managing Director of Respondent Company). Respondents are Vijay Khanna & Ors (Petitioners). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute arising from non-compliance with NCLT orders dated 2013-06-10 and an undertaking dated 2014-08-14 in Company Petition No. 69/2003. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence showed the Appellant paid the Rs. 5 lakh cost and tendered an unconditional apology in person, which was accepted by the Respondents. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT originally passed an order on 2017-04-13 in Contempt Petition No. 3(ND)2017, imposing a Rs. 5 lakh cost and ordering one-month simple imprisonment of the Appellant. The Appellant appealed this contempt order.
legal_issues: Whether the punishment of imprisonment and attachment of property for contempt should be set aside given the contemnor's subsequent compliance and unconditional apology.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Contempt penalties may be modified or set aside if the contemnor purges the contempt by fully complying with the original order, paying imposed costs, and tendering an unconditional apology. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal relied on the mutual admission by both parties that the previous orders had been fully complied with and costs paid. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The tribunal concluded that since the appellant purged the contempt and apologized, the punitive directives of imprisonment and asset attachment were no longer warranted.
operative_order: The NCLAT modified the NCLT's impugned order by setting aside the portions directing the attachment/sale of property, simple imprisonment of one month for the Appellant, and the issuance of arrest warrants. No costs.
summary: Vinod Kumar Kapoor, Managing Director of the respondent company, appealed an NCLT order that found him guilty of contempt. The NCLT had imposed a cost of Rs. 5 lakhs, directed the attachment of his assets, and sentenced him to one month of simple imprisonment for failing to comply with prior orders and undertakings. During the appeal, both parties confirmed that the appellant had fully complied with the original tribunal orders and paid the Rs. 5 lakh cost. The appellant also tendered an unconditional apology in person. Taking this compliance into account, the NCLAT modified the NCLT order, setting aside the imprisonment and asset attachment directives.

case_title: K. Raghavendra Rao vs Lakshmi Vilas Bank & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is K. Raghavendra Rao (Corporate Debtor representative). Respondent is Lakshmi Vilas Bank (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying debt owed to Lakshmi Vilas Bank. State Bank of India was also involved as an interested party attempting to bail out the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount not explicitly quantified in the order, but default was established. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant claimed an ongoing dispute but admitted there was nothing on record to support the existence of such a dispute. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Lakshmi Vilas Bank filed under Section 9 IBC. NCLT Chennai admitted the application on 2017-08-17. The Appellant appealed against this admission.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in admitting the Section 9 application when the Corporate Debtor claimed an ongoing dispute but provided no evidence on record.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for insolvency resolution cannot be rejected on the mere assertion of a dispute if there is no evidence on record to substantiate its existence prior to the filing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The tribunal interpreted 'existence of dispute' strictly, requiring tangible evidence on record rather than mere oral assertions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The bench evaluated the case records and found zero documentary evidence supporting the appellant's claim of a pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Section 9 application was complete and there was no record of a dispute, the NCLAT concluded that the NCLT rightfully admitted the application.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT Chennai order admitting the Section 9 application. The tribunal clarified that the dismissal would not prevent the Appellant from settling with the Operational Creditor and seeking appropriate relief from a competent court.
summary: K. Raghavendra Rao appealed the NCLT Chennai's decision to admit a Section 9 insolvency application filed by Lakshmi Vilas Bank. Initially, there was confusion whether the application should have been under Section 7 or 9, but it was pursued under Section 9. The appellant alleged a pre-existing dispute and stated that State Bank of India was negotiating to bail out the corporate debtor. However, the NCLAT noted that the Section 9 application was complete and the appellant failed to produce any evidence on record demonstrating a pre-existing dispute. Consequently, the NCLAT found no flaw in the Adjudicating Authority's decision and dismissed the appeal, leaving room for a future settlement.

case_title: S3 Electrical & Electronics Private Limited vs Brian Lau
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is S3 Electrical & Electronics Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). Respondent is Brian Lau (Claimed Operational/Financial Creditor). Andhra Bank is the Appellant in the connected appeal. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An 'Unsecured Loan Agreement dated 18th June, 2014' existed between the parties. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount not explicitly quantified; Respondent claimed default based on the unsecured loan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondent produced the Unsecured Loan Agreement and communications but failed to produce the specific records of default prescribed by the IBBI. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed under Section 7 IBC. NCLT New Delhi admitted the application on 2017-06-28 ex-parte (without notice to the Corporate Debtor). Corporate Debtor and its banker (Andhra Bank) appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an insolvency application under Section 7 can be admitted without issuing notice to the Corporate Debtor and without providing the specific evidence of default prescribed by the IBBI.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Admitting an insolvency petition without providing prior notice to the Corporate Debtor violates the principles of natural justice and renders the admission order invalid. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 initiation requires the specific documents prescribed by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India; alternative documents cannot substitute the prescribed evidentiary requirements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal found the admission flawed because the creditor relied on an Unsecured Loan Agreement instead of the mandatory IBBI-prescribed default records, and the debtor was not heard. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT's ex-parte admission violated natural justice and lacked appropriate statutory evidence, warranting the setting aside of the order.
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's order dated 2017-06-28, dismissing the Section 7 application. All actions taken by the Interim Resolution Professional were declared illegal. The Corporate Debtor was released from the CIRP rigors to function independently. The Corporate Debtor was directed to pay the fees of the IRP. No costs.
summary: S3 Electrical & Electronics Pvt. Ltd. and its banker, Andhra Bank, appealed the NCLT New Delhi's admission of a Section 7 insolvency petition filed by Brian Lau. Lau claimed a default based on a 2014 Unsecured Loan Agreement. The NCLAT discovered that the Adjudicating Authority admitted the petition and initiated the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process without issuing any notice to the Corporate Debtor, clearly violating the principles of natural justice. Furthermore, Lau failed to submit the mandatory records of default as specified by the IBBI. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeals, set aside the NCLT's order, dismissed the Section 7 application, and restored the Corporate Debtor's management.

case_title: Madhukar Tulsi vs Ajay Kumar Gupta & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Madhukar Tulsi (Director of Corporate Debtor, IERO Fiveriver Pvt. Ltd.). Respondents are Ajay Kumar Gupta and Mrs. Poonam Gupta (Financial Creditors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial debt owed by IERO Fiveriver Pvt. Ltd. to the Respondents. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount not explicitly specified. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The parties reached a post-admission settlement agreement on 2017-11-18. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents filed a Section 7 application which NCLT New Delhi admitted on 2017-11-13. The Appellant appealed, seeking disposal based on a subsequent settlement.
legal_issues: Whether an admitted insolvency application can be withdrawn or set aside by the Appellate Tribunal based on a post-admission settlement between the parties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the IBC framework, an insolvency application cannot be withdrawn once it has been admitted by the Adjudicating Authority, even if the parties reach a settlement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench interpreted Rule 8 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016, strictly, concluding that the Adjudicating Authority's power to permit withdrawal is expressly limited to the period before admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal acknowledged the valid settlement dated 2017-11-18 but determined it was legally immaterial to overturning a legally sound admission order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded it lacked the statutory power to accept the post-admission settlement and interfere with an otherwise legally sound NCLT admission order.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal with no costs, stating no relief could be granted despite the settlement. The tribunal noted this order would not prevent the appellant from seeking appropriate relief from the Supreme Court under its inherent powers.
summary: Madhukar Tulsi, Director of IERO Fiveriver Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT New Delhi's order admitting a Section 7 insolvency petition filed by Ajay Kumar Gupta and Poonam Gupta. After the petition's admission on November 13, 2017, the parties reached a settlement on November 18, 2017. The appellant requested the NCLAT to dispose of the appeal based on this settlement. However, citing Rule 8 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016, the NCLAT held that an application cannot be withdrawn post-admission. Finding no illegality in the original admission order, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal, directing the appellant to seek relief from the Supreme Court.

case_title: Nooruddin Khan & Anr vs Himayat All Khan & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Nooruddin Khan & Anr. Respondents are Himayat All Khan & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over company management and authorized legal representation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A Board resolution dated September 22, 2016 authorized Sachin S. Shetye to represent the company. A subsequent rival resolution on April 3, 2017 authorized Nooruddin Khan, who engaged A.V. Nishanth. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru passed an order on April 28, 2017 in C.P. No. 10/2016 rejecting Mr. A.V. Nishanth's mandate to represent the company, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal correctly recognized the legal representative appointed by the earlier board resolution amidst an ongoing management dispute.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In cases of management dispute, the person originally authorized by the first undisputed board resolution should represent the company until that resolution is legally annulled. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Priority and validity of the earliest unchallenged board resolution prior to the management fracture. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal upheld the NCLT's decision allowing the originally authorized representative to proceed, dismissing the rival faction's appointee.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as having no merit. No order as to costs.
summary: In an appeal regarding company representation amidst a management dispute, the NCLAT reviewed competing board resolutions. The original resolution dated September 2016 authorized one representative, while a later April 2017 resolution by a rival group authorized another. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT Bengaluru's decision to recognize the representative appointed under the first resolution, noting that the earlier mandate had not been legally recalled. The appeal was dismissed with no costs.

case_title: M/S Raipur Power & Steel Ltd. & Ors vs Tomorrow Sales Agency Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Raipur Power & Steel Ltd. Respondent/Creditor is Tomorrow Sales Agency Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debt obligation owed by the corporate debtor to the financial creditor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Remaining principal sum of Rs. 8,82,00,000. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Seven demand drafts totaling Rs. 8,82,00,000 were handed over in court, plus Rs. 10,50,000 deducted as TDS. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appeal filed against insolvency proceedings to facilitate a full and final settlement.
legal_issues: Whether insolvency proceedings can be closed upon the corporate debtor making full and final payment of all dues to the financial creditor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal may dispose of insolvency appeals and direct the adjudicating authority to close proceedings if the corporate debtor pays all outstanding dues. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Physical handover of demand drafts in open court satisfying the creditor's full claim. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since full payment was made to the financial creditor, the tribunal found it appropriate to direct the closure of proceedings subject to verification.
operative_order: Appeal stands disposed of. The Tribunal is directed to close the proceedings and release the corporate debtor from the rigors of law if it verifies that all financial and operational creditors have been paid. No costs.
summary: Raipur Power & Steel Ltd. appealed against insolvency proceedings initiated by Tomorrow Sales Agency Pvt. Ltd. During the appeal, the appellant handed over demand drafts totaling Rs. 8.82 crores as full and final payment to the financial creditor. Acknowledging this settlement, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal and directed the NCLT to close the insolvency proceedings and restore the company's independent management once all creditor dues were verified as paid.

case_title: Shri Ramesh Chander Goel & Ors vs M/S Dinesh International Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Shri Ramesh Chander Goel & Ors (former respondents 3, 4 & 6). Respondents are M/s Dinesh International Ltd., Daya Kishan Goel & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Formation of a joint venture consortium requiring a Rs. 20 crore deposit with Indian Railways. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Extra Ordinary General Meetings were held on April 1 and April 25, 2006. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The 40% shareholder group was not served notice for the EGM, resulting in oppression and company business coming to a standstill. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT set aside the EGM resolutions on February 2, 2017, due to mismanagement. Appellants appealed solely against the tribunal's observations regarding their mismanagement.
legal_issues: Whether general observations by the tribunal regarding gross mismanagement by specific directors render the underlying judgment illegal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: General observations of mismanagement by directors in charge of company affairs do not invalidate an otherwise lawful tribunal order. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of the company's operational standstill and the dissipation of its assets, which indicated gross mismanagement. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found no grounds to interfere with the NCLT's findings of mismanagement against the directors who were managing the company's affairs.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, declining to interfere with the impugned judgment dated February 2, 2017. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellants challenged an NCLT order that struck down 2006 EGM resolutions for being oppressive to 40% shareholders. The appellants, who were directors at the time, specifically contested the NCLT's observations that their actions amounted to gross mismanagement. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's findings, stating that the company's subsequent financial deterioration and standstill justified the observations against the directors in charge. The appeal was dismissed with no costs.

case_title: Macks Hard Pvt. Ltd. & Anr vs Mrs. Uma Chamanlal Anand & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Macks Hard Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. Respondents are Mrs. Uma Chamanlal Anand & Ors (legal heirs of the deceased member). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Transmission of shares and payment of unclaimed dividend belonging to Late Shri. Chamanlal Anand. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Approximately Rs. 6 crores lying in unclaimed dividend accounts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A pay order transferring the Rs. 6 crores was issued in the name of the respondents. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai ordered a monthly disbursement of Rs. 2 lakhs to the petitioner pending resolution. Appellants challenged this interim direction.
legal_issues: Whether the interim order for monthly disbursement requires modification following the company's transfer of the total unclaimed dividend to the legal heirs.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate courts can dispose of appeals via consent orders and grant liberty to modify lower tribunal orders if parties mutually resolve the underlying financial trigger. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Acknowledgment by both counsels that the Rs. 6 crores had been transferred via pay order to the respondents. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the dividend was fully paid out, the appellate tribunal allowed the appellants to seek modification of the original interim order at the NCLT.
operative_order: Appeal disposed of by consent. The appellant is granted liberty to approach the NCLT Mumbai for modification of the March 10, 2017 order regarding the monthly disbursement. No costs.
summary: Macks Hard Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Mumbai interim order directing the company to pay Rs. 2 lakhs monthly to the legal heirs of a deceased shareholder. During the proceedings, the company transferred approximately Rs. 6 crores of unclaimed dividend to the heirs. Recognizing this development and with the respondents' consent, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal. The tribunal granted the company liberty to file a fresh application before the NCLT to modify the original monthly payment order, issuing no costs.

case_title: Anu Elastics Pvt. Ltd. vs Aggarwal Elastics
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Anu Elastics Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and Respondent is Aggarwal Elastics (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods where the Operational Creditor raised invoices, but the Corporate Debtor claimed goods were defective and returned. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed principal amount of Rs. 47,56,651.50 and interest of Rs. 46,03,115/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Legal notice issued by Operational Creditor on 2016-03-09, replied to by Corporate Debtor on 2016-06-01. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor produced the 2016-06-01 reply letter disputing the debt and asserting return of defective goods. Furthermore, the postal tracking report showed the NCLT notice was returned as 'No such office at the given address'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 9 application on 2017-07-25, deeming notice served despite the return report, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a returned postal notice marked 'No such office at the given address' constitutes valid service, and whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC can be admitted when there is a pre-existing dispute regarding defective goods.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Return of notice for insufficient or wrong address cannot be deemed as valid service, unlike a deliberate refusal by a party. Furthermore, an insolvency application must be rejected if there is clear evidence of a pre-existing dispute prior to the filing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Service of notice is a fundamental requirement of natural justice under the IBC, and a deemed service cannot be presumed on a returned tracking report stating 'No such office'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal examined the tracking report to find service was invalid, and evaluated the reply letter dated 2016-06-01 to establish a bona fide pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the NCLT order violated natural justice due to lack of service and wrongly admitted the petition despite a clear pre-existing dispute, thus setting the order aside.
operative_order: The NCLT's admission order dated 2017-07-25 is set aside, and the Section 9 application is dismissed. All actions taken by the Interim Resolution Professional are declared illegal, and the Corporate Debtor's board is restored to function independently. Respondents are directed to pay the fees of the IRP, with no order as to costs.
summary: Anu Elastics Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi's admission of a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by Aggarwal Elastics. The NCLAT observed two fatal flaws in the NCLT's decision. First, the NCLT wrongly deemed the notice served despite the postal tracking report indicating 'No such office at the given address', which violated the principles of natural justice. Second, a reply letter from the Corporate Debtor dated June 1, 2016, clearly established a pre-existing dispute over defective goods and denied liability for the claimed Rs. 47,56,651 principal. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the admission order, and restored the Corporate Debtor's independent management.

case_title: N. Kasthur Reddy vs Prakjyothi Constructions Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is N. Kasthur Reddy. Respondents are Prakjyothi Constructions Pvt. Ltd. and other individuals (Respondent Nos. 4 to 13). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management and shareholding of the Respondent Company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant was illegally removed from the register of members on 2013-03-22. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant's name was removed on 2013-03-22, and during his illegal exclusion, the company increased its authorized share capital, made new allotments to Respondents 6 to 13, and executed sale deeds without notice to him. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad on 2017-03-20 found oppression, restored the Appellant's membership, and set aside share transfers to Respondents 4 and 5, but failed to grant relief regarding the subsequent share capital increase and allotments.
legal_issues: Whether a member who was illegally removed and later restored is entitled to consequential relief invalidating subsequent share allotments and capital increases made without notice during the period of illegal exclusion.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a member is illegally removed and later restored to status quo ante, subsequent corporate actions such as share capital increases and allotments made without notice to the excluded member must also be set aside as consequential relief. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal verified that the allotments and capital increases occurred during the intervening period of the appellant's illegal exclusion and were challenged in the original petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that restoring the member's status required setting aside all intervening capital increases and share allotments made in his absence.
operative_order: The NCLAT modified the NCLT's order dated 2017-03-20 by setting aside all share allotments and authorized share capital increases made in favor of Respondents 6 to 13 during the intervening period. Respondents were directed to rectify the register of members within one month. No costs were awarded.
summary: N. Kasthur Reddy appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order that restored his membership but failed to invalidate corporate actions taken during his illegal exclusion. The Appellant was unlawfully removed from the company's member register on March 22, 2013. While the NCLT correctly restored his position, it did not address the subsequent increase in authorized share capital and share allotments made to Respondents 6 to 13 without notice to the Appellant. The NCLAT modified the NCLT order, holding that true restoration of status quo ante required setting aside those intervening share allotments and capital increases, directing the company to rectify its register within one month.

case_title: M/S. Eicher Motors Limited vs Adesh Kaur & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s. Eicher Motors Limited. Respondents are Adesh Kaur & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Shareholding records and portfolio management of the company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT made passing observations against the appellant company without relying on specific records while granting 6 weeks' time for compliance. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Company Petition No. 8/59/2015 is pending adjudication before the NCLT New Delhi; Eicher Motors appealed against the interim remarks made by the Tribunal.
legal_issues: Whether passing adverse observations against a party without basing them on records during an interim phase of a pending company petition is sustainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adverse observations made against a party without backing from concrete records should not prejudice rights, and the adjudicating authority must decide the core case purely on merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: SEBI can take steps under law against any party provided it strictly adheres to the principles of natural justice and statutory guidelines. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of the interim order indicated that remarks were passed without concrete evidence or final findings on record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the lower tribunal did not issue final definitive directions or interim prejudice other than granting time for steps, the appeal was disposed of with directions for an uninfluenced expeditious hearing.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of. The NCLT is directed to hear and decide the main company petition on merits uninfluenced by any prior observations, ensuring an early disposal. No costs.
summary: M/s Eicher Motors Limited appealed against an interim order passed by NCLT New Delhi in a pending company petition, which included adverse remarks against the company while granting time to ensure specific steps.
