The NCLAT noted that the observations were not grounded in formal records and that the main petition was still pending adjudication. Declining to interfere with the timeline extension, the Appellate Tribunal disposed of the appeal with instructions that the NCLT must proceed and decide the case strictly on its merits without being influenced by the initial remarks, with no order as to costs.

case_title: Export-Import Bank of India vs Resolution Professional Jekpl Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Export-Import Bank of India (Exim Bank). Respondent is the Resolution Professional of JEKPL Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process initiated against the Corporate Debtor (JEKPL Pvt. Ltd.) under Section 10 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Resolution Professional objected to Exim Bank's inclusion in the Committee of Creditors, prompting a series of interim and remand directions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Exim Bank previously filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 188 of 2017, where the NCLAT remitted the matter back to the NCLT Allahabad Bench. Subsequently, the Adjudicating Authority shifted the decision back to the RP and CoC via order dated October 27, 2017, triggering the current appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can abdicate its statutory power by delegating the final determination of a creditor's status to the Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority cannot abdicate its adjudicatory responsibilities by shifting core legal decisions onto the Resolution Professional or the Committee of Creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Statutory determinations regarding creditor status and committee membership must be adjudicated directly by the NCLT rather than delegated internally. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the lower tribunal's order confirmed that it improperly remitted a judicial issue back to administrative agents (RP/CoC). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Adjudicating Authority must directly decide the continuity of Exim Bank as a Committee of Creditors member without relying on delegated reports.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of, directing the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Allahabad) to immediately decide the question of Exim Bank's continuity as a CoC member within three weeks, uninfluenced by any reports from the RP or CoC. No costs.
summary: Export-Import Bank of India appealed against an order passed by NCLT Allahabad, which had delegated the decision of whether to admit Exim Bank into the Committee of Creditors back to the Resolution Professional and the CoC. Reviewing the matter, the NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority cannot abdicate its core legal duties by asking administrative entities to decide judicial questions. The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by directing the NCLT to independently decide Exim Bank's status as a CoC member within three weeks, with no order as to costs.

case_title: Balraju Sunkari & Ors vs N. Sekhar Reddy & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Balraju Sunkari & Ors. Respondents are N. Sekhar Reddy & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate management dispute and internal company proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Previous Company Petition No. 55 of 2014 was withdrawn with leave to file afresh, leading to Company Petition No. 74/241/HDB/2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Company Application No. 136/2017 was filed objecting to the maintainability of the main petition, which the NCLT disposed of while scheduling the main matter for final hearing. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad passed an interim order on July 28, 2017, directing comprehensive replies and scheduling the matter, which the appellants challenged on grounds of natural justice.
legal_issues: Whether an interim order disposing of an objection application and directing comprehensive replies while setting a final hearing date violates procedural fairness.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicating body may decline to evaluate piecemeal objections and instead direct comprehensive pleadings to ensure expeditious final adjudication of a dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of the impugned order confirmed that the NCLT explicitly kept all doors open for the appellants to file comprehensive replies and raise all contentions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found no procedural flaw or prejudice since the appellants retained the full right to submit comprehensive replies and defend their case on merits.
operative_order: The appeal is rejected as devoid of substance, affirming the NCLT's interim order and procedural directions.
summary: Balraju Sunkari and others appealed against an interim order passed by NCLT Hyderabad, which disposed of their maintainability objection application and posted the main company petition for final hearing. The appellants argued they were denied adequate opportunity to contest the preliminary issues. The NCLAT observed that the NCLT's order explicitly directed the respondents to file a comprehensive reply addressing all allegations, keeping all legal contentions open for the appellants. Finding no denial of natural justice, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: KKV Naga Prasad vs. Lanco Infratech Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant KKV Naga Prasad was an employee/operational creditor, and Respondent Lanco Infratech Ltd. was the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment relationship and associated dues. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified claimed dues, later settled via a total of Rs. 15 lacs and a Mercedes Car. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not explicitly detailed in text, except the lower tribunal order date of 21st February 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Payment receipts showing Rs. 15 lacs paid during appeal and a Mercedes car given towards full and final dues. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Original application under Section 9 of the I&B Code was rejected by the NCLT Hyderabad Bench on 21st February 2017 on the ground that it cannot go into a roving enquiry into disputed claims.
legal_issues: Whether the appeal against the rejection of a Section 9 application should be permitted to be withdrawn following an amicable settlement between an employee-appellant and the corporate debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal may permit the withdrawal of an insolvency appeal when parties arrive at an amicable settlement during proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The court acknowledged the settlement of dues under the framework of the Code without settling deeper questions of disputed employee claims on merits. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Acceptance of voluntary part payments and transfer of assets (car and cash) as evidence of amicable settlement negotiations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench permitted the withdrawal of the appeal with liberty to the appellant to raise claims before a court of competent jurisdiction or an IRP if future insolvency proceedings are initiated.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn with liberty granted to the appellant to raise claims, if any due, before a Court of Competent Jurisdiction or before an Interim Resolution Professional if insolvency is initiated. No costs.
summary: This appeal arose from an NCLT Hyderabad Bench order rejecting the appellant's Section 9 application against Lanco Infratech Ltd. During the appellate proceedings, the parties reached an amicable settlement wherein the corporate debtor paid Rs. 15 lacs and provided a Mercedes car toward full and final dues. Consequently, the appellant sought permission to withdraw the appeal. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as withdrawn, granting the appellant liberty to pursue claims before a court of competent jurisdiction or an Interim Resolution Professional if future insolvency proceedings are initiated.

case_title: Ravi Rajnish & Anr. vs. Jain Link Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Ravi Rajnish and Archana Rajnish were shareholders; Respondent No. 1 was Jain Link Pvt. Ltd., alongside individual respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Shareholding rights and corporate management of the company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (oppression and mismanagement petition involving stolen/unaccounted shares). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: FIR lodged for stolen shares on 28.01.2007; original petition C.P. No. 151 of 2015 filed in 2015. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pleadings showing appellants knew of alleged illegal acts and loss of shares in 2007, and stock transfer by appellant No.1 to his mother on 15.09.1997. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Company Petition No. 151 of 2015 was filed claiming oppression and mismanagement; NCLT allowed Company Application No. 1231 of 2015 filed by the respondent, dismissing the appellants' claim on grounds of delay and laches.
legal_issues: Whether a company petition alleging oppression and mismanagement filed nearly eight years after discovering the loss of shares and corporate changes is barred by delay and laches.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Claims regarding corporate oppression and mismanagement brought after a massive and unexplained delay, where petitioners had long-standing knowledge of the facts, are barred by laches. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Evaluation of limitation and laches principles in company law petitions concerning historical share transfers and director appointments. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented evidence showing knowledge of the dispute dating back to 2007 and a 1997 share transfer nullified claims of active, continuous grievance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly applied the doctrine of delay and laches to dismiss a belated company petition filed in 2015 regarding acts known since 2007.
operative_order: The appeal is rejected, confirming the NCLT order allowing Company Application No. 1231 of 2015 and dismissing the main company petition.
summary: Appellants appealed an NCLT order dismissing their Company Petition No. 151 of 2015, which alleged oppression, mismanagement, and missing shareholding dating back to 2007. The NCLAT noted that the appellants had knowledge of the alleged illegal acts and loss of shares since 2007 and that appellant No. 1 had transferred shares in 1997, yet waited until 2015 to file the petition. Finding no error in the NCLT's application of delay and laches, the Appellate Tribunal rejected the appeal.

case_title: Paramjeet Singh vs. Maxim Tubes Company Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Paramjeet Singh was the Director of the Corporate Debtor (M/s. International Coil Limited), while the 1st Respondent was Maxim Tubes Company Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods or services forming an operational debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified debt amount default leading to Section 9 application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Operational creditor issued a demand notice under Section 8(1); the corporate debtor failed to dispute the claim or submit a reply under Section 8(2) within the statutory 10-day period. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 5 application stating no objection was filed by the corporate debtor under Section 8(2), and disputed letters alleged to be forged. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Special Bench, New Delhi, admitted the Section 9 application on August 16, 2017, issued a moratorium, and appointed an Interim Resolution Professional.
legal_issues: Whether a corporate debtor can raise the defense of a pre-existing dispute in an appeal when it failed to file any reply or raise a dispute within 10 days of receiving a Section 8 demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a corporate debtor fails to respond to a Section 8 demand notice or raise a pre-existing dispute within the statutory 10-day timeline, it cannot subsequently derail a Section 9 admission on those grounds. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict adherence to the mandatory operational workflow and timelines specified under Section 8(2) and Section 9 of the I&B Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Absence of any timely written notice of dispute or reply under Section 8(2) submitted to the operational creditor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The adjudicating authority's admission of the Section 9 application was legally sound given the corporate debtor's default in responding to the statutory demand notice.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT order admitting the Section 9 application, imposing a moratorium, and appointing the IRP.
summary: The appellant, a director of the corporate debtor, challenged an NCLT order admitting a Section 9 application filed by an operational creditor. The NCLAT observed that although the appellant claimed an existing dispute, the corporate debtor had completely failed to reply to the Section 8 demand notice or raise any dispute within the statutory 10-day window. Consequently, the appellate tribunal found no merit in the appeal and dismissed it, affirming the initiation of the corporate insolvency resolution process.

case_title: West Bengal Essential Commodities Supply Corporation Ltd. vs. Bank of Maharashtra
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant West Bengal Essential Commodities Supply Corporation Ltd. was a State Government undertaking/corporate debtor, and Respondent Bank of Maharashtra was the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit/loan facility default. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount of Rs. 27.93 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Principal Bench order passed on May 29, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Complete and defect-free application filed by the financial creditor under Section 7 of the I&B Code. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench admitted the Section 7 application on May 29, 2017, declared a moratorium, ordered public announcements, and appointed an Interim Resolution Professional.
legal_issues: Whether ongoing settlement talks or the status of a corporate debtor as a State Government undertaking dealing with farmers provide legal grounds to interfere with a complete and valid Section 7 insolvency admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Ongoing settlement negotiations or public utility status do not bar the admission of a complete Section 7 application under the I&B Code, provided the debt and default are established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Mandatory admission of a Section 7 application when a financial debt is proven and the application is complete, without extraneous economic considerations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of completeness and absence of defects in the financial creditor's Section 7 petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The adjudicating authority committed no error in admitting the application, though settlement avenues remain open post-constitution of the Committee of Creditors.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of, upholding the admission order, with the clarification that if the appellant settles the dues of Rs. 27.93 crores and satisfies all other creditors, it may request the Adjudicating Authority to close the resolution process.
summary: The appellant, a State Government undertaking, challenged an NCLT order admitting a Section 7 insolvency application filed by the Bank of Maharashtra for a default of Rs. 27.93 crores. The appellant argued that settlement talks were underway and that it supplied essential commodities to farmers. The NCLAT held that these grounds do not warrant interfering with a valid admission order. However, the tribunal clarified that the appellant could seek closure of the resolution process from the Adjudicating Authority if it successfully settled with all creditors during the proceedings.

case_title: Asomi Industries Pvt. Ltd. vs. Sashi Kumar Tea Co. Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant was Asomi Industries Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent Nos. 5 & 6 (Petitioners before the Tribunal) were directors/shareholders, alongside Sashi Kumar Tea Co. Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance, board management, and company administration of a tea company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (corporate mismanagement and board resolution dispute). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board meeting and contested resolution passed on September 19, 2014; subsequent board meetings held thereafter; NCLT Guwahati Bench order passed on March 3, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate records, board resolutions, records of employee wage payments, statutory dues, and fixed deposits. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati Bench held the removal of Respondent Nos. 5 & 6 under the resolution dated September 19, 2014, to be illegal, set aside that resolution, restored them as directors, and declared all subsequent board meetings and actions void and illegal.
legal_issues: Whether setting aside subsequent board meetings due to the illegal removal of directors should invalidate legitimate administrative actions such as employee wage payments, statutory dues, and fixed deposits executed during that interim period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While resolutions passed in the absence of illegally removed directors are rightly set aside, routine administrative actions safeguarding company interests, employee wages, and statutory dues taken during the interim period should be legally saved. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Equitable balance under company law to rectify mismanagement without inflicting collateral damage on innocent third parties, workmen, and statutory authorities. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of corporate actions post-September 19, 2014, distinguishing between governance takeovers and bona fide operational payments. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's order is modified to preserve all operational, statutory, and employee-related actions taken by the company during the interim period.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of, and the NCLT Guwahati Bench order dated March 3, 2017, in CP No. 182/2014 is modified by saving all actions taken by the company pursuant to board meetings held after September 19, 2014, relating to employees, workmen, payment of wages, statutory dues, and fixed deposits. No order as to costs.
summary: The appellant challenged an NCLT Guwahati Bench order which set aside a September 2014 resolution, restored two directors, and voided all subsequent board meetings. While agreeing with the restoration of directors, the appellant argued that invalidating subsequent meetings canceled essential wage payments, statutory dues, and fixed deposits. The NCLAT modified the NCLT order to preserve all bona fide actions relating to employees, wages, statutory dues, and fixed deposits taken during the interim period, ensuring the company's operational continuity remains protected.

case_title: Astra Offshore Sdn Bhd vs. Swiber Offshore (India) Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant was Astra Offshore Sdn Bhd (operational creditor), and the Respondent was Swiber Offshore (India) Pvt Ltd (corporate debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of offshore marine/oilfield services and supplies. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified debt amount default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Another Section 9 petition filed by Mr. Ajay Joseph (Global Marine Supply Company) was admitted by the NCLT Mumbai Bench on 31.03.2017 (CP No. 51/I&BP/NCLT/MAH/2017). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 31.03.2017 declaring a moratorium, imposing prohibitions on suits/asset transfers, and appointing Mr. Rajeev Mennadiar as Interim Resolution Professional. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the separate insolvency petition against the corporate debtor on 31.03.2017, prompting the appellant to seek withdrawal of its own pending appeal to approach the IRP.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw its pending appeal to file claims before the Interim Resolution Professional when a corporate insolvency resolution process has already been initiated against the corporate debtor by another creditor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a corporate insolvency resolution process is already active against a corporate debtor under the Code, subsequent or parallel appellate proceedings by other creditors can be withdrawn to enable claimants to file their claims directly before the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Respecting the moratorium and collective resolution framework established under Sections 13, 14, and 31 of the I&B Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verified existence of an active admission order and moratorium passed by the NCLT Mumbai Bench in a concurrent petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant is permitted to withdraw the appeal to pursue claims before the IRP, without the appellate tribunal deciding on the merits of the underlying debt entitlement.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of as withdrawn with liberty granted to the appellant to move before the Interim Resolution Professional to raise its claim. No costs.
summary: The appellant filed an appeal against the corporate debtor, Swiber Offshore (India) Pvt Ltd. During the proceedings, it was brought to notice that another Section 9 petition filed by Global Marine Supply Company had already been admitted by the NCLT Mumbai Bench on March 31, 2017, initiating a moratorium and appointing an IRP. Consequently, the appellant sought permission to withdraw the appeal to file its claim before the IRP. The NCLAT allowed the withdrawal with liberty to approach the IRP, leaving the determination of the debt amount to the appropriate resolution authorities.

case_title: Diamond Engineering (Chennai) vs. Shah Brothers
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant was Diamond Engineering (Chennai) (Corporate Debtor), and Respondent was Shah Brothers (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of engineering services/contractual work. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified default amount leading to Section 9 application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Chennai passed the admission order on June 6, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forms 3 and 5 signed by a director of the operational creditor company; records showing no prior objection was raised by the appellant before receiving the Section 8 notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Chennai admitted the operational creditor's Section 9 petition on June 6, 2017, declared a moratorium under Section 14, and appointed an Interim Resolution Professional.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application is maintainable when notices and forms are signed by a company director and whether allegations of forged bills can be raised for the first time without prior response to the Section 8 notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any authorized person connected with the operational creditor company, including a director, is competent to issue a demand notice under Section 8 and file a petition under Section 9 of the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of Form 3 and Form 5 rules under the I&B Code permitting authorized company representatives/directors to initiate actions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Absence of any timely objection or dispute raised by the corporate debtor prior to the receipt of the Section 8 statutory notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: New pleas regarding forged documents and improper bank certificates not raised before the adjudicating authority cannot be entertained, and the admission order stands.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as lacking in merit, upholding the NCLT Chennai order admitting the Section 9 application, imposing a moratorium, and appointing the IRP.
summary: The corporate debtor appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dated June 6, 2017, which admitted a Section 9 insolvency application filed by Shah Brothers. The appellant argued that the bills were forged and that Forms 3 and 5 were not signed by a properly authorized person. The NCLAT found that the forms were signed by a director of the company who was legally competent to act, and noted that no dispute had been raised prior to the Section 8 notice. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Satish Mittal vs. Ozone Builders & Developers Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant was Satish Mittal (advance-paying homebuyer/claimant), and Respondent was Ozone Builders & Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Advance cash deposit of Rs. 30 lacs made on February 22, 2013, for booking a plot in Ozone City, Aligarh, with a term for refund without interest if booking was unconfirmed within one year. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure to refund the advance amount of Rs. 30 lacs after booking non-confirmation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Receipt issued on February 22, 2013; NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi order passed on April 24, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Cash receipt dated February 22, 2013, showing advance payment for a plot booking without any formal purchase agreement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench rejected the appellant's Section 9 application on April 24, 2017, holding that the appellant did not qualify as an 'Operational Creditor'.
legal_issues: Whether a person who advanced money for a real estate plot booking under a receipt lacking a formal purchase agreement qualifies as an 'Operational Creditor' under Section 5(20) and Section 5(21) of the I&B Code.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advance payment made for a property booking based merely on a receipt, without the provision of goods, services, employment, or government dues, does not constitute an 'operational debt' and the claimant is not an 'operational creditor'. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict construction of Section 5(20) and Section 5(21) defining operational creditors and operational debts to exclude general financial advances or real estate deposits. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the receipt demonstrating a cash deposit for a plot booking rather than a claim arising from goods, services, or statutory law. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The adjudicating authority correctly rejected the Section 9 application because the appellant's claim did not fall within the definition of operational debt.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, affirming the NCLT rejection order.
summary: The appellant challenged an NCLT Principal Bench order rejecting his Section 9 application against Ozone Builders & Developers Pvt. Ltd. The appellant had deposited Rs. 30 lacs in 2013 for booking a plot, which was never confirmed or refunded. The NCLAT held that since the appellant did not supply goods, render services, or fall under any employment or statutory dues category, he did not qualify as an operational creditor under Section 5 of the Code. The appeal was accordingly dismissed.

case_title: Kapil Gupta & Anr. vs. Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants were Kapil Gupta & Anr. (representing the corporate debtor Deltronix India Ltd., which was transposed as 2nd Respondent), and 1st Respondent was Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial loan facility default. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified debt amount default leading to Section 7 application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi order passed on November 24, 2017; settlement attempted after the admission order. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Records showing a post-admission settlement agreement with only part payment made. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench admitted the Section 7 application on November 24, 2017, initiated the resolution process, declared a moratorium, and appointed an Interim Resolution Professional.
legal_issues: Whether an insolvency application under Section 7 can be withdrawn or set aside based on a settlement reached between the parties *after* the formal admission of the application by the adjudicating authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once an application under Section 7 of the Code is admitted and corporate insolvency resolution process is initiated, neither the financial/operational creditor nor the adjudicating authority/appellate tribunal has the jurisdiction to withdraw the application or recall the admission order based on a subsequent settlement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict interpretation of Rule 8 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016, restricting withdrawal requests to the pre-admission stage. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that the settlement occurred after the admission order and involved only part payment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The admission order cannot be annulled based on a post-admission settlement, though operational guidelines must be maintained to keep the company as a going concern.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The Resolution Professional must ensure the company remains ongoing, authorize the suspended board or authorized persons to sign cheques only under RP approval, and permit day-to-day operations, vendor bill payments, employee salaries, and utility bills. No costs.
summary: Appellants challenged an NCLT order admitting a Section 7 insolvency petition filed by Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. The appellants sought to set aside the process due to a post-admission settlement. The NCLAT held that under Rule 8 of the 2016 Rules, an application cannot be withdrawn after admission, and neither the adjudicating authority nor the appellate tribunal has jurisdiction to recall an admission order based on post-admission settlements. The appeal was dismissed with directions ensuring the company's day-to-day operations and salary disbursements continue under the IRP's oversight.

case_title: PEC Ltd. vs. M/s. Sree Ramakrishna Alloys Ltd. (Along with Company Appeal No. 121 of 2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant was PEC Ltd. (Financial Creditor), and Respondent was M/s. Sree Ramakrishna Alloys Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) [along with M/s. Sree Gangadhar Steels Ltd. in Appeal No. 121 of 2017]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Extension of financial loan by way of Inland Letter of Credit (ILC). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed principal amount of Rs. 10,35,95,033 plus interest of Rs. 4,80,31,874, totaling Rs. 15,16,26,907. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority passed orders on July 29, 2017, adjourning the matters to August 29, 2017, to allow the corporate debtor to submit payment modalities. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pleadings and memos regarding proposed payment modalities and employment stakes. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Hyderabad Bench adjourned the Section 7 applications instead of admitting or rejecting them outright on July 29, 2017, prompting the financial creditor to appeal against the delay.
legal_issues: Whether an adjudicating authority commits a reversible error by granting a brief, one-time adjournment to a corporate debtor to settle outstanding dues before deciding on the admission or rejection of a Section 7 insolvency application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicating authority may grant a limited opportunity or adjournment to a corporate debtor to explore settlement or present payment modalities before deciding on the admission of a Section 7 or Section 9 application, provided it adheres to statutory timeframes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Review of the discretionary powers of the Adjudicating Authority under the I&B Code prior to formal admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of whether the adjournment granted was excessive or intended to protect worker employment while balancing creditor claims. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal will not interfere with a short adjournment order aimed at settlement, provided the adjudicating authority decides the case expeditiously without granting further extensions.
operative_order: Both appeals are disposed of without interfering with the adjournment orders dated July 29, 2017, with the expectation that the NCLT Hyderabad will not grant further time and will decide the applications either way on the next date.
summary: PEC Ltd. appealed against NCLT Hyderabad orders adjourning its Section 7 insolvency petitions against two corporate debtors to allow them time to settle dues and protect employee interests. The appellant contended that the authority was bound to immediately admit or reject complete petitions. The NCLAT declined to interfere with the brief adjournment granted to explore settlement possibilities, but expressed trust that the adjudicating authority would strictly decide the cases on the next hearing date without granting further extensions.

case_title: Nityanand Singh and Co. vs. Ferrous Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Nityanand Singh and Co. was the Operational Creditor, and Respondent was Ferrous Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of operational goods, services, or associated dues. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified default amount leading to Section 9 application rejection. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on September 28, 2017; certified copy applied for on October 30, 2017; appeal filed on November 27, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Presence of the appellant's company secretary during the delivery of the September 28, 2017 order and subsequent delay records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority rejected the Section 9 application on September 28, 2017, and the appellant filed the appeal after sixty days from the date of the order.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal filed after sixty days from the date of the impugned order can be entertained when Section 61(2) specifies a thirty-day limitation period extendable by a maximum of fifteen days.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal filed beyond the combined statutory period of thirty days plus the maximum permissible grace period of fifteen days cannot be condoned, as the tribunal lacks jurisdiction to extend time past forty-five days. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict computation of limitation under Section 61(2) of the I&B Code and its proviso. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Calculation of days elapsed from the pronouncement date of the impugned order to the actual filing date after defect removal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appeal was preferred after sixty days, the application for condonation of delay is dismissed and the appeal is time-barred.
operative_order: The application for condonation of delay is dismissed, and consequently, the appeal is dismissed as being barred by limitation. No costs.
summary: The operational creditor appealed against an NCLT order dated September 28, 2017, which rejected its Section 9 application. The appeal was filed after sixty days from the date of the order without a valid explanation for the delay. The NCLAT held that under Section 61(2) of the Code, the tribunal has no jurisdiction to condone a delay exceeding fifteen days beyond the initial thirty-day appeal period. Consequently, the delay condonation application and the appeal were dismissed as time-barred.

case_title: Lotus Homes Ltd. & Ors. vs. Sanjan Kumar Bhagat & Ors. (Along with Company Appeal Nos. 225 & 226 of 2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants were Lotus Homes Ltd., UCIC Pvt. Ltd., and Kamini Ferro Ltd. along with others; Respondents were Sanjan Kumar Bhagat & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate proceedings, pleadings management, and procedural compliance before the tribunal. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (procedural appeal regarding rejoinder filing and document service). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lower tribunal orders passed on May 16, 2017, concerning delayed rejoinders and unsigned demurrers. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tribunal records showing rejoinder filed on May 9, 2017, without leave and service of an unsigned, un-notarized reply. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT took a delayed rejoinder on record subject to a cost of Rs. 3,000 payable to the State Legal Service Authority, West Bengal, and directed the petitioner to supply exact copies of replies.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal should interfere with interlocutory procedural orders directing the submission of exact copies of replies and imposing costs for delayed rejoinder filings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate courts generally refrain from interfering with routine discretionary interlocutory orders managing procedural timelines and compliance within lower tribunals. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Evaluation of NCLT procedural rules regarding timely filing and service of pleadings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of record showing late filing of rejoinders without leave and service of unauthenticated copies. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: No legal infirmity exists in the NCLT's conditional acceptance of pleadings and direction to supply proper copies, warranting dismissal of the appeals.
operative_order: All three appeals are dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants challenged identical NCLT orders dated May 16, 2017, which accepted a delayed rejoinder subject to a cost of Rs. 3,000 payable to the State Legal Service Authority and directed the supply of exact copies of replies. The NCLAT found no ground to interfere with the procedural directions issued by the adjudicating authority and dismissed all the appeals.

case_title: Ashok Mittal & Anr. vs. Uniworth Resorts Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants were Ashok Mittal & Anr.; Respondents included Uniworth Resorts Limited & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate ownership, management, and associated company disputes. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (delay condonation application in a company appeal). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on May 5, 2017; certified copy application filed on May 19, 2017, and issued on June 23, 2017; appeal filed on August 8, 2017, following a holiday on August 7, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certified copy records indicating dates of application and issuance, alongside NCLAT office order declaring Raksha Bandhan holiday on August 7, 2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellants filed an application (I.A. No. 558 of 2017) seeking condonation of delay in filing the appeal against the May 5, 2017 order.
legal_issues: Whether a delay in filing an appeal should be condoned when计算 from certified copy issuance dates and affected by declared public holidays falls within the permissible discretionary condonation window.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Delay in filing an appeal may be condoned in the interest of justice when the computation falls within the discretionary statutory condonation limits of the appellate tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Assessment of limitation periods taking into account certified copy preparation timelines and intervening official holidays. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of filing dates, certified copy issuance logs, and official tribunal holiday notifications. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the time calculation falls within the condonable period and serves the interest of justice, the delay stands condoned.
operative_order: The delay condonation application (I.A. No. 558 of 2017) is allowed, the delay is condoned, and the appeal shall be taken up for regular consideration.
summary: Appellants filed an application to condone the delay in filing Company Appeal (AT) No. 268 of 2017 against an order dated May 5, 2017. The respondents contested the computation of limitation, while the appellants pointed to certified copy issuance dates and an intervening holiday on August 7, 2017. The NCLAT held that even under strict calculations, the delay fell well within the period that the tribunal has the power to condone. Consequently, the delay was condoned in the interest of justice and the application was disposed of.

case_title: Hero Motorcorp Ltd. vs. Kashyap D. Chokshi & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant was Hero Motorcorp Ltd.; Respondents were Kashyap D. Chokshi & Anr. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate shareholding management and transfer of unclaimed shares. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (interim order regarding transfer of unclaimed shares to Investor Education and Protection Fund). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Interim order passed by NCLT Principal Bench on October 27, 2017; next hearing fixed for November 7, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Terms of the interim order restraining share transfer to the IEPF and requiring shares to be held with the company pending reply. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench passed an interim order on October 27, 2017; the appellant sought to challenge it via appeal before seeking permission to withdraw.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal should interfere with an interim order restraining a company from transferring unclaimed shares to the Investor Education and Protection Fund when proceedings are still pending before the lower tribunal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate tribunals will not interfere with interim preservation orders passed by lower tribunals when parties have been granted time to file replies and the main matter is pending adjudication. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Review of discretionary interim powers of the National Company Law Tribunal under company law. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the interim injunction terms and the procedural posture showing pending reply filing dates. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: No valid grounds exist to interfere with the interim order, and the appellant's request to withdraw the appeal must be granted without liberty to re-litigate the same issue.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn, without any liberty to challenge the same order before the Appellate Tribunal. No costs.
summary: Hero Motorcorp Ltd. appealed against an interim order dated October 27, 2017, passed by the NCLT Principal Bench, which restrained the company from transferring unclaimed shares and dividends to the Investor Education and Protection Fund. Finding no grounds to interfere with an interim order where the appellant had sought time to file a reply below, the NCLAT permitted the appellant to withdraw the appeal. The appeal was accordingly dismissed as withdrawn without liberty.

case_title: Smt. Poonam Gupta & Ors. vs. Shardul Vikram Gupta (In Contempt Petitions Nos. 2, 3, and 4 of 2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicants were Smt. Poonam Gupta & Ors.; Contemner/Respondent was Shardul Vikram Gupta (Director of AJ Prakashan Pvt. Ltd. and other entities). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Compliance with appellate tribunal inspection orders regarding company premises and records. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (alleged willful disobedience of NCLAT order dated March 2, 2017). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellate order passed on March 2, 2017; Supreme Court extension order passed on May 8, 2017; contempt petitions listed on July 20, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Affidavits of unconditional apology, explanations regarding subordinate actions under a bona fide belief, and records of written intimations for inspection. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Contempt notices were issued on April 25, 2017; the contemner filed affidavits of apology and stated readiness to cooperate with inspections under Supreme Court directions.
legal_issues: Whether contempt proceedings should be pursued or dropped when a contemner tenders an unconditional and unqualified apology and undertakes full cooperation with court-mandated inspections.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Contempt proceedings may be closed upon the acceptance of a sincere, unconditional, and unqualified apology coupled with demonstrated compliance and an undertaking to cooperate with judicial directions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Exercise of contempt jurisdiction with an emphasis on purging contempt through compliance rather than punitive measures. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of the contemner's personal appearance, affidavit statements, and willingness to facilitate company record inspections pursuant to higher court extensions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The unconditional apology is accepted, personal appearance is dispensed with, and contempt petitions are disposed of with a warning regarding future compliance.
operative_order: All three contempt petitions are disposed of. The personal appearance of the contemner, Shri Shardul Vikram Gupta, is dispensed with, accepting his unconditional apology with the caveat that future violations will invite strict penal action without leniency.
summary: Applicants filed contempt petitions alleging willful violation of the NCLAT's order dated March 2, 2017, which permitted inspection of company premises. The contemner, Shri Shardul Vikram Gupta, appeared in person, filed affidavits containing an unconditional and unqualified apology, explained that subordinate actions stemmed from a bona fide misunderstanding, and noted that inspection timelines had been extended by the Supreme Court. The NCLAT accepted the unconditional apology, dispensed with the contemner's further appearance, and closed the contempt petitions with a strict warning regarding future compliance.

case_title: Bindeshkumar Balvantbhai Thakkar vs. ROC, Ahmedabad & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bindeshkumar Balvantbhai Thakkar and Girishbhai Amratbhai Patel were the Appellants, while ROC, Ahmedabad & Ors. were the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate compliance and regulatory matters involving the Registrar of Companies. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (regulatory/company appeal). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not specifically detailed, aside from the hearing date of October 6, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Statements made by counsels confirming that an out-of-court settlement had been achieved between the parties. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appeals were preferred before the NCLAT, where counsels for both appellants and respondents reported that the underlying disputes had been completely settled.
legal_issues: Whether appeals should be permitted to be withdrawn when the contesting parties have amicably settled their disputes.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate tribunals will permit the withdrawal of appeals when all contesting parties confirm that an amicable settlement of the dispute has been reached. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Facilitating amicable resolutions and settlement-based closures in company law proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Joint statements and concurrence from counsels representing both the appellants and the Registrar of Companies confirming settlement. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the parties settled the dispute, both appeals can be disposed of as withdrawn.
operative_order: Both appeals (Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 259 and 260 of 2017) are disposed of as withdrawn.
summary: Appellants Bindeshkumar Balvantbhai Thakkar and Girishbhai Amratbhai Patel filed appeals against the Registrar of Companies, Ahmedabad & Ors.. During the proceedings, the respective counsels for the appellants and respondents informed the bench that the underlying dispute had been settled. With no opposition from the Registrar of Companies, the NCLAT disposed of both appeals as withdrawn.

case_title: IVRCL Limited vs. Sanghvi Movers Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant was IVRCL Limited (Corporate Debtor), and Respondent was Sanghvi Movers Limited (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of equipment/services leading to an operational debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified default amount leading to Section 9 application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned NCLT order passed on September 27, 2017; fresh Section 9 application filed by operational creditor on November 8, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Records showing failure to comply with Section 8 procedural requirements in the initial petition, prompting a withdrawal request. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench noticed lack of compliance with Section 8 in C.P. No. 117/9/HDB/2017 and allowed the operational creditor time to issue a fresh demand notice; the corporate debtor appealed against this order.
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor can withdraw a defective Section 9 application before the appellate tribunal to rectify procedural omissions under Section 8 and file a fresh petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor is permitted to withdraw a pending insolvency application that lacks proper Section 8 compliance, with liberty to issue a fresh demand notice and institute a new petition upon default. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Mandatory pre-requisites of issuing a valid demand notice under Section 8 prior to maintaining an application under Section 9 of the I&B Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that the initial application suffered from non-compliance with statutory notice requirements under Section 8. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The operational creditor's request to withdraw the defective application must be granted to enable compliance with statutory procedures.
operative_order: The application filed under Section 9 before the Adjudicating Authority is dismissed as withdrawn with liberty to the operational creditor as prayed for, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to close C.P. No. 117/9/HDB/2017 accordingly, with no order as to costs.
summary: IVRCL Limited (Corporate Debtor) appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad Bench order which found that Sanghvi Movers Limited had filed a Section 9 petition without complying with Section 8 of the I&B Code. During the appeal, the operational creditor sought permission to withdraw the application to issue a fresh demand notice and file a new petition. The NCLAT granted the withdrawal request, dismissed the original Section 9 application as withdrawn with liberty to re-file, and directed the adjudicating authority to close the case.

case_title: Vijay Prasad vs M/s IDIO Construction & Industries
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Vijay Prasad and the Respondent is M/s IDIO Construction & Industries. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not specified in the order other than a defective appeal filing. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not specified. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The appeal was filed on March 29, 2017, with a delay of 54 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Not detailed; defects included incomplete pagination, unverified declaration, missing memo of parties, and lack of appellant signature. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Filed as a defective appeal on March 29, 2017, and dismissed by the NCLAT on April 25, 2017, due to incurable defects and being barred by limitation.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal filed with multiple procedural defects and a delay of 54 days can be entertained.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal suffering from fundamental procedural defects and statutory time-bars that cannot be condoned is liable for dismissal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Limitation periods prescribed by law must be strictly adhered to, and delays beyond condonable limits cannot be excused. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of proper formatting, correct signatures, structured pagination, and adherence to limitation rules. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was dismissed because it was both defective in presentation and time-barred by a 54-day delay that could not be condoned.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed being defective and barred by limitation.
summary: This case involves an appeal filed by Vijay Prasad against M/s IDIO Construction & Industries before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal. The appeal suffered from severe procedural defects including incomplete pagination, absence of proper signatures, and a lack of a memo of parties. Furthermore, it was barred by limitation with an un-condonable delay of 54 days. Consequently, the appellate tribunal dismissed the appeal entirely on grounds of defects and limitation.

case_title: Radheshyam Fibres Pvt. Ltd. vs State Bank of India
appeal_number: I.A. No. 750 of 2017 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 187 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The original appellant was Radheshyam Fibres Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), the respondent was State Bank of India, and the applicant for substitution was Popatbhai Ramjibhai Bhalara (shareholder). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution process initiated by a financial creditor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly detailed in this interim application order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Interlocutory application filed following a recent Supreme Court precedent. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Reliance placed on the Supreme Court decision in Innoventive Industries Ltd. vs. ICICI Bank and Ors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An interlocutory application was filed to substitute a shareholder as the appellant and transpose the original corporate debtor as the second respondent.
legal_issues: Whether a shareholder of a corporate debtor can be substituted as an appellant in place of the corporate debtor following recent Supreme Court jurisprudence.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An aggrieved shareholder of a corporate debtor is permitted to maintain an appeal and be substituted as an appellant when supported by binding judicial precedent. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of standing for stakeholders to challenge insolvency admission orders under statutory frameworks. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Satisfaction of valid grounds for substitution based on established Supreme Court rulings regarding corporate debtor representation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The application for substitution is allowed, replacing the corporate debtor appellant with its shareholder and transposing the original corporate debtor as a respondent.
operative_order: The application for substitution (I.A. No. 750 of 2017) is allowed. Mr. Popatbhai Ramjibhai Bhalara is substituted as the appellant, and Radheshyam Fibres Pvt. Ltd. is transposed as the 2nd Respondent through the Interim Resolution Professional.
summary: This interlocutory application before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal dealt with a substitution request in an insolvency appeal involving Radheshyam Fibres Pvt. Ltd. and State Bank of India. Citing the Supreme Court's ruling in Innoventive Industries Ltd. vs. ICICI Bank, a shareholder of the corporate debtor, Popatbhai Ramjibhai Bhalara, sought to replace the corporate debtor as the appellant. The tribunal found the grounds satisfactory, allowed the substitution, and transposed the original corporate debtor as the second respondent through its Interim Resolution Professional.

case_title: Sri Haridas Pottath vs Peerless Engineering Products Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Sri Haridas Pottath and the Respondents are Peerless Engineering Products Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute arising from company law matters culminating in an impugned order dated August 29, 2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on August 29, 2017; appeal heard and disposed of on November 10, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Oral arguments presented before the tribunal indicated the likelihood of a dismissal on merits. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant chose to withdraw the appeal after initial arguments when the tribunal indicated a reasoned dismissal order was imminent.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw an appeal unconditionally after facing adverse observations during initial arguments.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant has the procedural autonomy to seek withdrawal of an appeal, which the court may grant with or without liberty. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Discretionary exercise of appellate powers upon oral request for withdrawal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluation of counsel submissions and judicial inclination during preliminary hearings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Permitting withdrawal of the appeal without granting liberty to challenge the underlying order again.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn with no order as to costs, and without liberty to file any appeal against the impugned order dated August 29, 2017.
summary: Sri Haridas Pottath filed an appeal against Peerless Engineering Products Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal challenging an order dated August 29, 2017. During the hearing, upon realizing that the tribunal intended to dismiss the appeal through a reasoned order, the appellant's counsel sought permission to withdraw it. The tribunal granted the request, dismissing the appeal as withdrawn without granting any liberty to file a subsequent appeal against the same order.

case_title: Welspum Enterprises vs ROC Gujarat & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Welspum Enterprises and the Respondents are ROC Gujarat & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Compounding of offenses under the Companies Act pursuant to proceedings before the NCLT, Ahmedabad Bench. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Compounding fee amount of Rs. 3,42,000/- ordered by the tribunal. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Extension of time sought to pay the compounding amount by May 31, 2017; original NCLT orders dated March 16, 2017, and April 17, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Submissions by counsel confirming readiness to pay the fine if timeline extensions are granted. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appeals filed against orders of the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in T.P. No. 149/621A/NCLT/AHM/2016, modified upon joint submission for time extension.
legal_issues: Whether appellate timelines for payment of compounding fees ordered by the NCLT can be extended upon request of the appellant.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate forums possess the authority to modify payment timelines and operational directives of lower tribunals when parties exhibit bona fide willingness to comply. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Construction of discretionary powers under company law appeals concerning compounding fees. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the appellant's undertaking to fulfill financial compliance through specific banking instruments. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The payment timeline is extended and the lower tribunal's order is modified accordingly to facilitate compliance.
operative_order: The appellants are allowed to pay the amount of Rs. 3,42,000/- by way of a Demand Draft from any nationalized bank in favor of the Pay and Accounts Officer, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Mumbai, by May 31, 2017. Orders dated March 16, 2017, and April 17, 2017, passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench stand modified accordingly.
summary: Welspum Enterprises filed appeals before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal seeking an extension of time to pay a compounding fine of Rs. 3,42,000/- mandated by the NCLT, Ahmedabad Bench under Section 621A of the Companies Act. With the appellant expressing readiness to pay, the NCLAT modified the lower tribunal's orders, granting an extension until May 31, 2017, for the payment to be made via demand draft to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.

case_title: Indian Bank vs M/s Cethar Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Indian Bank and the Respondents are M/s Cethar Ltd. & Ors. (including 1st, 2nd, and 5th respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency resolution proceedings involving a corporate debtor and financial creditor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not specified in the withdrawal order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appeal listed and disposed of on November 23, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Instructions received by counsel directly from bank officials to withdraw the matter. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant bank sought withdrawal of the insolvency appeal, to which opposing respondents raised no objection.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant financial creditor can withdraw its insolvency appeal upon instructions from its management when no opposing party objects.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will permit the unconditional withdrawal of an appeal when the master of the suit (appellant) voluntarily chooses not to press it and respondents express no objection. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Exercise of inherent withdrawal powers in corporate insolvency appellate proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Confirmation of instructions from institutional client officials to counsel. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal stands dismissed as withdrawn based on the appellant's own volition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn. No order as to costs.
summary: Indian Bank filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 140 of 2017 before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal against M/s Cethar Ltd. & Ors. During the proceedings, the counsel for the appellant stated that he had direct instructions from the bank's officials to withdraw the appeal. As the respondents raised no objections to this course of action, the NCLAT formally dismissed the appeal as withdrawn without any order as to costs.

case_title: Dr. V. Shankar vs M/s Deccan Chronicle Holdings Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Dr. V. Shankar and the First Respondent is M/s Deccan Chronicle Holdings Ltd. & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company petition matters pending before the National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi, bearing C.P. No. 05(IND)/2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Order issued on March 27, 2017, referencing a prior order dated March 9, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Submissions made by counsel Mr. Ajit Sharma, Mr. Harsha Reddy, Mr. Alok Dhir, and others regarding pending petitions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal filed against an NCLT order where the appellate tribunal declined to interfere, granting liberty to bring relevant precedents to the notice of the tribunal for potential transfer.
legal_issues: Whether the appellate tribunal should interfere with an NCLT order when a similar matter is covered by a prior decision of the appellate tribunal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate court will decline to interfere with a tribunal order if the subject matter can be appropriately addressed by transferring the case based on existing precedents. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Proper application of administrative transfer mechanisms for similar company petitions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of whether the cause is covered by the coordinate bench's decision dated March 9, 2017. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is disposed of without interference, leaving the parties to seek transfer before the tribunal while preserving the respondents' right to withdraw writ petitions.
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of with observations that the parties may bring the relevant order to the notice of the Tribunal for potential transfer, and the order will not bar respondents from withdrawing the writ petition to raise contentions before the competent Tribunal.
summary: Dr. V. Shankar filed an appeal against M/s Deccan Chronicle Holdings Ltd. & Ors. challenging an order passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal declined to interfere with the impugned order, noting that if the case was covered by a previous decision dated March 9, 2017, the parties could request a transfer to the appropriate bench. The appeal was accordingly disposed of with these observations, preserving the right of respondents to raise their contentions before the competent forum.

case_title: Shri Manish Vipinchandra Patel & Anr. vs Ambika Food Product Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Shri Manish Vipinchandra Patel & Anr. and the Respondents are Ambika Food Product Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company law dispute involving corporate management or operations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Hearing conducted and order passed on September 18, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Non-appearance of the appellants despite repeated calls during the court session. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appeal was called out multiple times, and due to continuous absence on behalf of the appellants while respondents were represented, the appeal faced dismissal for lack of prosecution.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal should be dismissed when the appellant fails to appear before the tribunal after multiple calls.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal is liable to be dismissed for non-prosecution if the appellant or their legal representation fails to appear when the matter is called for hearing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Exercise of inherent powers of the appellate tribunal to clear pending matters marked by default of appearance. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of repeated calls and presence or absence of parties on record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Dismissal of the appeal due to the total absence of the appellants during the proceedings.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for non-prosecution.
summary: Shri Manish Vipinchandra Patel & Anr. filed Company Appeal (AT) No. 306 of 2017 against Ambika Food Product Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal. When the matter was called repeatedly on September 18, 2017, nobody appeared for the appellants, whereas Respondents Nos. 2 and 3 were represented by their authorized representative, Shri Ashok Mehta. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal for non-prosecution.

case_title: James Hotels Limited vs Punjab National Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is James Hotels Limited and the Respondent is Punjab National Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency and debt resolution dispute arising from financial credit facilities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not specified in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appeal heard and disposed of on June 1, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consent given by the opposing counsel reflecting no objection to the withdrawal request. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant's counsel sought permission to withdraw the appeal during the hearing, which was granted without granting liberty to challenge the same order again.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw an insolvency appeal when the respondent expresses no objection, and under what conditions liberty to re-file should be denied.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant may withdraw an appeal upon request, and the appellate court may restrict granting liberty to re-initiate challenges against the same impugned order. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Application of procedural withdrawal rules in insolvency appellate proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Lack of objection from the contesting respondent. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is disposed of as withdrawn without granting liberty to file subsequent challenges against the same order.
operative_order: The appellant is allowed to withdraw the appeal without any liberty to move against the same very impugned order. The appeal stands disposed of as withdrawn.
summary: James Hotels Limited filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insol.) No. 46 of 2017 against Punjab National Bank before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal. During the hearing on June 1, 2017, the learned counsel for the appellant requested permission to withdraw the appeal. Since the respondent raised no objections, the NCLAT permitted the withdrawal, disposing of the appeal without granting any liberty to challenge the underlying impugned order again.

case_title: 3A Capital Services Ltd vs SRPM Ltd & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is 3A Capital Services Ltd and the Respondents are SRPM Ltd & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute concerning share certificates and corporate securities transfer. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Proceedings heard and concluded on May 4, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Submissions by counsel indicating a desire to approach ICICI Bank for share certificate revalidation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After initial arguments, the appellant requested withdrawal to pursue administrative remedies with a bank regarding share transfers.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal can be withdrawn to enable the appellant to seek administrative revalidation of share certificate transfers from a financial institution.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant is permitted to withdraw an appeal to pursue alternative administrative or institutional remedies such as share revalidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Facilitating out-of-court or institutional resolution of corporate securities disputes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of counsel's submissions during initial arguments. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is disposed of as withdrawn with directions enabling the appellant to approach the bank.
operative_order: The appellant is allowed to withdraw the appeal to enable them to move before ICICI Bank for revalidation of the transfer of share certificates. The appeal stands disposed of with the aforesaid directions.
summary: 3A Capital Services Ltd filed Company Appeal (AT) No. 144 of 2017 against SRPM Ltd & Ors. before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal. Following initial arguments on May 4, 2017, the appellant's counsel sought permission to withdraw the appeal so the company could approach ICICI Bank for the revalidation of the transfer of share certificates. The NCLAT granted the request and disposed of the appeal with those specific directions.

case_title: Shree Hanuman Foundry Engineering Co. Ltd. & Ors. vs Murari Mohan Kejriwal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Shree Hanuman Foundry Engineering Co. Ltd. & Ors. and the Respondent is Murari Mohan Kejriwal. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance and meeting directives issued during company law proceedings before the NCLT Kolkata Bench. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appeal heard and decided on July 6, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Impugned order direction requiring the company to convene an Annual General Meeting. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal was brought challenging the NCLT Kolkata Bench's direction to hold an AGM, which the appellate tribunal found legally sound upon review.
legal_issues: Whether a direction by the NCLT requiring a company to hold an Annual General Meeting suffers from legal infirmity.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Directives issued by a tribunal ordering a company to fulfill statutory obligations such as holding an Annual General Meeting are valid and free from legal infirmity. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Enforcement of statutory corporate governance duties under company law frameworks. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of the lower tribunal's operational directives regarding company meetings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Finding no legal error in the mandate to hold an AGM, the appellate tribunal confirmed the lower order and dismissed the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. No orders as to costs.
summary: Shree Hanuman Foundry Engineering Co. Ltd. & Ors. filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 190 of 2017 against Murari Mohan Kejriwal before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, challenging an order of the NCLT, Kolkata Bench, which directed the company to hold an Annual General Meeting. The NCLAT found no infirmity in the lower tribunal's directive requiring compliance with corporate meeting requirements and accordingly dismissed the appeal with no orders as to costs.

case_title: Navdisha Real Estate Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. GPI Textiles Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Navdisha Real Estate Pvt. Ltd. & Ors., and the Respondents are GPI Textiles Ltd. & Ors. (including Respondent Nos. 1 and 9). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance and company petition disputes. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appeal heard and disposed of on October 4, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Submissions made by counsel for the appellants seeking to withdraw with liberty to initiate contempt proceedings or file a fresh company petition. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellants sought and were granted permission to withdraw the appeal during initial arguments, with the tribunal expressing no opinion on future actions.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw a company appeal with liberty to initiate contempt proceedings or file a fresh company petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant is entitled to withdraw an appeal, and the appellate court may grant liberty to pursue other remedies without expressing any view on the merits of those future actions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Exercise of discretion in permitting withdrawal of company law appeals. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of counsel's submissions requesting voluntary withdrawal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn, leaving all future remedies open without judicial endorsement of their merits.
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of as withdrawn with liberty to the appellants to move an application for initiation of contempt proceedings and/or to file another company petition, without expressing any opinion on merits.
summary: Navdisha Real Estate Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. filed Company Appeal (AT) No. 315 of 2017 against GPI Textiles Ltd. & Ors. After brief arguments on October 4, 2017, the appellants' counsel requested permission to withdraw the appeal with liberty to file a contempt application or a fresh company petition. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal permitted the withdrawal while declining to express any opinion on the merits of future proceedings.

case_title: Origin Foods Ltd. vs. Axis Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Origin Foods Ltd., the 1st Respondent is Axis Bank Ltd., and the 2nd Respondent is Pudumjee Pulp & Paper Mills Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debt and financial facilities subject to an application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly specified in terms of exact monetary default figures in the short order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Order issued on August 18, 2017, following submissions to withdraw from a Section 7 application. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Submissions by the 2nd Respondent's counsel regarding the intent to withdraw as an applicant from the Section 7 insolvency petition before the Adjudicating Authority, Chennai Bench. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal arising from proceedings where the 2nd Respondent sought permission to withdraw its application before the Adjudicating Authority.
legal_issues: Whether a co-applicant can withdraw its application under Section 7 of the IBC, 2016, before the Adjudicating Authority and reserve rights to initiate independent legal action.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party is permitted to withdraw its application filed under Section 7 of the IBC, 2016, and such withdrawal does not bar it from subsequently approaching appropriate forums for relief if statutory criteria are met. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of withdrawal rights and creditor standing under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the applicant's intent to withdraw and preservation of the opposing party's right to contest. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is disposed of by allowing the withdrawal of the underlying Section 7 application while safeguarding all legal defenses and future rights of the parties.
operative_order: The 2nd Respondent is allowed to file a petition for withdrawal of the application, and the Adjudicating Authority, Chennai Bench, shall dispose of it as withdrawn and close the proceeding, with liberty preserved for future actions.
summary: Origin Foods Ltd. filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insol.) No. 86 of 2017 against Axis Bank Ltd. & Anr. During the hearing, the counsel for the 2nd Respondent (Pudumjee Pulp & Paper Mills Limited) stated its intention to withdraw as an applicant from the Section 7 IBC application pending before the NCLT Chennai Bench. The NCLAT permitted the withdrawal and directed the Adjudicating Authority to close the proceedings, clarifying that this would not prevent the 2nd Respondent from seeking appropriate legal remedies in the future while preserving the appellant's right to contest.

case_title: Raaj Bardhan Jayaswal vs. Kunal Bardhan Jayaswal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Raaj Bardhan Jayaswal, and the Respondents are Kunal Bardhan Jayaswal & Ors. (including Respondent Nos. 1 and 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company law dispute and internal management issues. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appeal heard and disposed of on April 20, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arguments presented by counsel for the appellant and various respondents (Mr. Anubhov Kumar, Mr. Raghav Sabharwal, Mr. Salim A Inamdar, and others). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following initial arguments, the appellant sought and was granted permission to withdraw the appeal to raise issues directly before the National Company Law Tribunal.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw an appeal to pursue contentions and issues before the National Company Law Tribunal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant may withdraw an appeal to re-agitate or raise all contentions before the primary adjudicating tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Directing parties back to the primary forum for comprehensive dispute resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of initial arguments and counsel's request for voluntary withdrawal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal stands dismissed as withdrawn with liberty granted to raise all issues before the NCLT.
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of as withdrawn with the liberty to raise all the issues and contentions before the National Company Law Tribunal.
summary: Raaj Bardhan Jayaswal filed Company Appeal (AT) No. 121 of 2017 against Kunal Bardhan Jayaswal & Ors. before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal. After some initial arguments on April 20, 2017, the appellant's counsel requested permission to withdraw the appeal. The NCLAT granted the request, disposing of the appeal as withdrawn while granting full liberty to the appellant to raise all contentions and issues before the National Company Law Tribunal.

case_title: Mr. Manan Chandraprakash Bhavsar vs. Hasmukh Bachubhai Holdings Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Manan Chandraprakash Bhavsar, and the Respondents are Hasmukh Bachubhai Holdings Ltd. & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company petition proceedings (C.P. No. 01/58-59/CLB/AHM/2015) before the National Company Law Tribunal, Ahmedabad Bench. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on February 27, 2017; appellate disposal on March 27, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Applications including IA No. 116/2016 and IA No. 9/2017 pending before the Tribunal for consideration. 6.
